scope: Introductory definitions and notation for reading the collection. Finite examples are identified explicitly. Each work retains its own definitions, hypotheses and evidence status.

background.papers: Vectors, matrices, linear maps, kernels and images, and reading a statement with hypotheses. Consult the selected paper for any additional algebra or analysis it uses.
background.monographs: Begin with the introduction and glossary. Then use the volume's own definitions to identify the background needed for its subject.
background.research: Read the problem statement, recorded scope and open questions first. The program's definitions determine its subject prerequisites.
background.packages: Basic command-line use and the package's programming language. Check its platform requirements before installation.
background.experiments: Basic programming and familiarity with the stated data and evaluation method. Read the input limits and acceptance criteria before interpreting output.

glossary.definition: A way to represent a declared system using concrete spaces and operations while respecting its required relations. A finite matrix realization assigns a space to each type and a matrix to each permitted arrow.
explanation: A realization gives an abstract specification something concrete to act on. The specification names objects, permitted operations and relations among compositions; the realization chooses spaces and actual maps that obey those relations. Merely drawing arrows or assigning matrices is insufficient if a required relation fails after the assignment.

For example, a specification with one arrow n and relation n²=0 can be realized by a nonzero square matrix N with N²=0. The relation constrains every input, not just one demonstrated vector. Different realizations can satisfy the same specification while having different dimensions, generating seeds, numerical conditioning or computational costs.

glossary.definition: Initial generating data from which the allowed operator action produces further elements. Whether a seed is sufficient depends on both the object and the declared action.
glossary.example_text: On R², let N(a,b) = (b,0) and v = (0,1). Then Nv = (1,0), so v and its image generate every vector by linear combinations.
explanation: A seed is useful because allowed operations can extract more information from it than scalar multiplication alone. Start with the seed, apply the declared legal operator words, and then form linear combinations of the resulting vectors. The size of that generated space depends on both the seed and the action.

With the identity as the only available operator, one seed spans at most one direction. If an operator swaps the two coordinates, the seed (1,0) also generates (0,1), so its operator-generated span is all of R². A claim about sufficient seeds must therefore specify the operator algebra rather than counting initial vectors in isolation.

glossary.definition: A label for a legal operator path or a packet coordinate. Examples include signal phases, residue classes, and positions in a packet tree. An address identifies a location in a representation, not necessarily a physical location.
explanation: An address tells a reader or algorithm where a component belongs in a declared representation. It can encode which operator path was followed, which residue phase was selected or which branch of a refinement tree was retained. The object stored at that address is separate from the label itself.

An address change can be a reversible reorganization without changing the represented data. Deleting an address, identifying several addresses or changing the permitted paths can instead lose distinctions. In a typed system, not every sequence of labels is a legal path: consecutive operations must also have compatible input and output types.

glossary.definition: A linear operator P satisfying P² = P. Applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once. This algebraic definition does not require orthogonality.
glossary.example_text: On R², P₁(a,b) = (a,0). Applying P₁ again still gives (a,0), so P₁² = P₁.
explanation: Idempotence means that every output of P is already settled: if y=Px, then Py=P²x=Px=y. Thus P acts as the identity on its image. Every vector splits algebraically as x=Px+(I−P)x, with the first part in im P and the second in ker P.

The kernel specifies the directions along which the projection is taken. Choosing a different complementary kernel can produce a different projector onto the same image. Orthogonal projection makes a particular choice using an inner product, whereas a general projector may amplify lengths and need not give an additive decomposition of squared energy.

glossary.definition: In the finite projector example, a selected component Pᵢx or the subspace in which it lies, according to context. Signal, algebraic and arithmetic works may assign the word more specific meanings.
glossary.example_text: For x = (2,3)ᵀ, the coordinate projectors give packets P₁x = (2,0)ᵀ and P₂x = (0,3)ᵀ. Their sum recovers x.
explanation: The packet language keeps track of a selected part of an object together with the rule selecting it. In a projector decomposition, Pᵢx is the actual packet value and im Pᵢ is its possible packet space. These are related objects, but a vector in a packet space is not the projector that selected it.

Completeness asks whether all retained packets reconstruct the original object. Transfer blocks then describe how an operation sends one packet into another. A packet decomposition need not be an eigenvector decomposition or an orthogonal split, so diagonal action and energy additivity require additional hypotheses stated in the relevant work.

glossary.definition: Values describing an object relative to a chosen representation. Coordinates can be unique basis coefficients or redundant measurements, depending on the setup.
glossary.example_text: The coordinate change C(a,b) = (a + b/2,b) sends x = (2,3)ᵀ to y = (7/2,3)ᵀ. These describe the same object in two coordinate systems.
explanation: A coordinate list is meaningful only with its decoding convention. In basis coordinates, every list represents one vector and every vector has one list. In redundant analysis coordinates, valid lists satisfy relations, and several arbitrary lists can synthesize to the same vector.

When a calculation moves between representations, carry the maps and their directions with the numbers. Matching list lengths is insufficient to show that two lists describe the same object. This is particularly important when one stage stores ordinary polynomial coefficients and another stores falling-factorial coefficients or packet measurements.

glossary.definition: Analysis sends an object to coordinates. Synthesis returns an object from coordinates. In the finite linear model, A and S are linear maps and exact reconstruction is the identity SA = I.
glossary.example_text: The analysis A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b) sends (2,3)ᵀ to (2,3,5)ᵀ. The example’s synthesis S returns (2,3)ᵀ, with SA = I₂.
explanation: Analysis describes what is measured or stored, while synthesis describes how those stored values are combined into an object. The order SA begins with an original vector, analyzes it and then reconstructs it. Exact reconstruction requires this composite to fix every vector in the stated input space.

The reverse order AS begins with a coefficient list. In a redundant representation it generally removes coefficient inconsistencies or gauge components instead of acting as the identity. Keeping these two spaces visible explains how exact object reconstruction can coexist with nonunique coefficient descriptions.

glossary.definition: The part of an operation connecting a source component to a target component. With source projector Pᵢ, target projector Qⱼ and operator T, the block is QⱼTPᵢ. Complete source and target families allow the blocks to reconstruct T.
glossary.example_text: For T = [[1,2],[3,4]], the coordinate block P₁TP₂ sends (2,3)ᵀ to (6,0)ᵀ. It carries source coordinate 2 into target coordinate 1.
explanation: Read QⱼTPᵢ from right to left: select input packet i, apply T, then retain output packet j. The two indices therefore name different roles, even when input and output spaces happen to coincide. A block may represent movement between scales, coordinates, phases or other declared components.

Summing every block reconstructs T when both projector families sum to their respective identities. Dropping cross-blocks asserts that some interactions are negligible or absent; the resulting residual must be checked. Diagonal packet blocks alone need not reproduce an operator that mixes the selected components.

glossary.definition: A compatible move from a coarser description to a finer one. In finite packet refinement, each fine packet has a coarse parent and each coarse projector is the sum of its children.
glossary.example_text: The zero-based even indices split into residue classes 0 and 2 modulo 4. Their selectors satisfy P₀ = F₀ + F₂.
explanation: Refinement records more detailed distinctions while retaining a rule for recovering the coarser description. In a packet tree, children belong to specified parents, and summing the children’s projectors recovers the parent projector. The extra detail is organized information rather than an unrelated second representation.

Compatibility must hold between levels, not merely within each separate level. Two individually valid decompositions may fail to form the claimed tower if their parent-child sums do not agree. Refining a description also does not guarantee convergence to an infinite limiting object; that requires separate analytic or structural conditions.

glossary.definition: A discrepancy computed for a specified identity or reconstruction. In Example 5 it is r = x − x̂. Other operations may use a different sign or norm, so the definition belongs with the reported number.
glossary.example_text: Dropping residue class 2 modulo 4 from (1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) gives r = (0,0,3,0,0,0,7,0). Its squared Euclidean norm is 58.
explanation: A residual measures failure of a particular equation or reconstruction, so its interpretation begins with that equation. The reconstruction residual x−x̂ differs from the equation residual b−Ax̂, even when both concern the same computed answer. Their signs, units and norms can also differ.

A small residual shows that the tested relation is nearly satisfied under its chosen measure. It does not automatically show that the computed answer is close to the desired answer: an ill-conditioned problem can turn a small equation residual into a large forward error. Recovering such a bound requires a stability estimate.

glossary.definition: An identified reason a requested construction cannot meet its stated conditions. In the recovery example, two inputs have the same coarse value but require different answers, so no recovery function from that value alone exists.
glossary.note: A nonzero numerical residual is not automatically a proof that every possible construction fails.
glossary.example_text: The inputs (1,0) and (0,1) have the same sum but different first coordinates. No function of their sum alone can return the first coordinate for every real input.
explanation: An obstruction excludes a requested construction throughout the stated class of possibilities. It therefore needs both a precise request and a reason that applies to every allowed candidate. A failed attempt, a large residual or a timeout identifies a problem with one method or run, but need not establish such a universal exclusion.

The recovery collision gives a particularly transparent obstruction. If two admissible inputs have the same summary and require different answers, a single function receiving that summary cannot return both. This proves impossibility for that summary and input class while leaving richer summaries or narrower input classes open.

glossary.definition: A structured report describing a particular check, with its evidence class, residuals, and assumptions. The producer determines what was checked. A saved certificate describes a past calculation and needs revalidation for a new one.
explanation: A certificate makes a check inspectable by recording what was tested, the assumptions used and the evidence returned. Its force comes from the checker’s contract and the validity of the recorded data, not from the file’s name or a success flag alone.

A numerical enclosure, a linear obstruction witness and a proof-path certificate therefore have different contents and implications. Check the input identity, source revision and evidence class before reusing one. Replaying a certificate can confirm its stated check without establishing additional modeling assumptions or broader mathematical claims.

glossary.definition: Computed or stated in exact algebra or arithmetic under the declared hypotheses. Exact rational arithmetic avoids rounding of those rational values. It does not establish an unchecked modeling assumption.
explanation: Exactness describes the arithmetic or equality being claimed, not the completeness of the entire investigation. Rational operations can retain fractions without rounding, and symbolic algebra can establish identities under explicit assumptions. These methods remove a particular source of numerical uncertainty.

The encoded problem can still differ from the intended model, omit cases or rely on an unproved premise. An exact calculation on sampled inputs also remains a finite calculation unless a general argument extends it. Read exact together with the domain, hypotheses and quantity actually computed.

glossary.definition: Computed with finite-precision arithmetic and interpreted using a stated error or residual rule. A zero observed floating-point residual does not turn the whole computation into an exact-arithmetic proof.
explanation: Numerical work approximates quantities using finite representations and algorithms. Its reliability depends on input interpretation, rounding, conditioning and approximation error, not merely on the number of printed digits. A reproducible numerical result should identify the relevant precision and acceptance rule.

Some numerical methods provide rigorous enclosures when their arithmetic and analytic remainders are controlled. Others provide estimates supported by residuals or convergence studies. These are different evidence classes. Repeated agreement or a displayed zero residual alone does not establish exact equality of the underlying mathematical objects.

glossary.definition: A result that retains explicitly listed assumptions. In a computation record, some of those assumptions may not have been established by the computation. Passing its checks does not discharge them.
explanation: A conditional theorem proves an implication: under the listed assumptions, the conclusion follows. The proof can be complete even when applying it to a particular example requires establishing assumptions that remain open or externally supplied.

Computation records need the same separation. A run may verify an algebraic step under a supplied bound without proving that bound. Reporting the final outcome should retain such dependencies explicitly. Calling a statement conditional does not itself say whether its assumptions are plausible, proved elsewhere or merely conjectured.

glossary.definition: A recorded connection between a written claim and a formal Lean statement. Compare hypotheses, the full formal type, source edition, and execution record. A similar declaration name or a working link alone does not establish the correspondence.
explanation: Correspondence concerns meaning between two statements, while Lean execution concerns checking the formal statement that was actually supplied. A successful kernel check does not by itself show that the formal types encode the intended objects, hypotheses and conclusion of the written theorem.

Compare the full declaration, imported assumptions and source edition with the relevant written passage. Also distinguish selected formal results from coverage of an entire work. A functioning source link or a similarly named declaration can help locate evidence, but cannot replace that comparison or an accepted execution record.

glossary.definition: A number from the declared coefficient field, used to multiply vectors. The hand-worked matrix examples use real scalars and exact rational entries.
glossary.quick_example: In 3(2,−1) = (6,−3), the number 3 is the scalar.
explanation: A scalar supplies the coefficients in a linear combination. In a₁v₁+a₂v₂, the a-values say how much of each vector to take, while the v-values are the objects being combined. Scalars can themselves be complex numbers or elements of a finite field; they need not be ordinary real measurements.

Always identify the coefficient field before dividing or solving a linear system. For example, division by 2 is available over the rationals but unavailable in characteristic two. Changing the field can therefore change which coordinate formulas are legal, even when the displayed matrix entries look identical.

glossary.definition: A number system with addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by every nonzero element. The rational, real, and complex numbers are examples. A result over one field does not automatically hold over another.
explanation: The division requirement is what makes ordinary linear algebra over a field especially flexible: every nonzero pivot can be normalized. A field has a zero element and a multiplicative identity, and those elements must differ. The integers fail the field condition because, for example, 2 has no inverse within the integers.

The chosen field affects more than arithmetic notation. A real rotation can acquire eigenvectors after extending the scalars to the complex numbers. Conversely, a construction that divides by an integer may fail in a finite field when that integer becomes zero. A theorem’s field hypothesis is part of its mathematical content.

glossary.definition: An element of a vector space. In the finite examples it is a column of numbers. Its coordinates depend on a chosen representation.
glossary.quick_example: The pair (2,3) and the polynomial 2+3x are vectors in different declared vector spaces.
explanation: The abstract object and its coordinate list are different things. A polynomial, a sampled signal and a column of numbers can each be vectors in an appropriate space. Once a basis is fixed, a coordinate list describes the object; choosing another basis changes that list without necessarily changing the object.

This distinction matters when comparing calculations in two representations. Before subtracting their coordinate columns, first put both columns in the same coordinate system. Otherwise an apparent discrepancy can come from comparing different descriptions rather than different vectors. The collection’s transfer and coordinate-change examples repeatedly use this separation.

glossary.definition: A collection of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication, with the usual distributive and associative laws. The space of pairs of real numbers is denoted R².
glossary.quick_example: Pairs (x,y) with x+y = 0 form a vector space; pairs with x+y = 1 do not contain zero.
explanation: The closure requirements mean that taking sums, differences and scalar multiples never leaves the space. A useful way to check a proposed example is to ask whether it contains zero and whether a general linear combination stays inside it. A plane through the origin can satisfy these conditions; a translated parallel plane generally does not.

Specifying the underlying set alone is insufficient: the scalar field and the addition and scaling operations also belong to the definition. In the finite examples, these choices let us speak consistently about kernels, bases and dimension. Other works may use spaces of functions or infinite sequences with additional analytic structure.

glossary.definition: A map T satisfying T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v) for all vectors u, v and allowed scalars a, b. A linear map preserves linear combinations.
glossary.quick_example: T(x,y) = (x+2y,3x) is linear. Adding a fixed nonzero offset would make it affine.
explanation: Linearity says that one can combine inputs before applying the map or combine their outputs afterward, with the same result. It implies T(0)=0 and makes the values on a basis sufficient to determine the entire map. This is why a finite matrix can encode an operation on infinitely many possible input vectors.

The identity must hold for every allowed linear combination, not just for a few test inputs. A map such as x↦x² can agree with a linear rule at selected points and still fail linearity elsewhere. Packet-by-packet reconstruction of an operation relies on this universal additivity, so nonlinear operations need a separate defect calculation.

glossary.definition: A rectangular array representing a linear map after bases have been chosen. An m by n matrix takes n coordinates to m coordinates. Each output coordinate is a row multiplied by the input column.
explanation: The columns of a matrix are the outputs of the input basis vectors, expressed in the output basis. Thus a matrix stores both an operation and the coordinate choices used to describe it. Multiplying by a column forms the corresponding linear combination of those stored output columns.

Dimensions keep the calculation meaningful: an m-by-n matrix accepts n coordinates and returns m. Changing the input or output basis changes the matrix through the appropriate coordinate maps. Properties such as injectivity belong to the represented map, whereas individual entries and many numerical norm values depend on its description.

glossary.definition: The map I that leaves every input unchanged, so Ix = x. The subscript in I₂ or I₃ specifies the dimension when needed.
glossary.quick_example: I₂(2,3) = (2,3). The identity is different from a matrix with every entry equal to one.
explanation: The identity is the neutral operation for composition: TI=T and IT=T whenever the types match. Its matrix has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere in any basis of the same space. The relevant space matters, because identities on different spaces are different typed maps.

Reconstruction formulas use the identity to say exactly what has been recovered. SA=I on the original object space means that every original input returns unchanged after analysis and synthesis. It does not also assert AS=I on a larger coefficient space. Keeping the identity’s domain visible prevents these two claims from being confused.

glossary.definition: All finite linear combinations of a specified set of vectors. The span of the empty set consists only of the zero vector. With an operator action, one may first apply allowed operators and then take the span.
glossary.quick_example: The span of (1,1) is the line {(a,a) : a is a scalar}.
explanation: A span is the collection of everything obtainable by the stated linear combinations, rather than merely the original list of vectors. Adding a vector already in that span does not enlarge it. Adding a vector outside it creates at least one new independent direction in the finite-dimensional setting.

In a seed calculation there are two stages: apply allowed operators to the seeds, then take linear combinations of the generated vectors. The initial seeds may be few even when their generated span is large. A span computation therefore answers a different question depending on whether operator action is allowed before combination.

glossary.definition: A family is linearly independent when the only linear combination giving zero has every coefficient zero. No member of a finite independent family can be formed from the others.
glossary.quick_example: (1,0) and (0,1) are independent, while (1,0) and (2,0) are dependent.
explanation: Independence is the uniqueness condition behind coordinates. If a nontrivial combination of the listed vectors is zero, the same vector can have two different coefficient lists: add that zero combination to any representation. Independence rules out precisely this ambiguity within the chosen family.

For finitely many columns, solving the homogeneous matrix equation tests independence: only the zero coefficient column should map to zero. A family can be independent without spanning the whole target space. To be a basis it must satisfy both requirements, so neither independence alone nor a large number of stored vectors is enough.

glossary.definition: A linearly independent spanning family. Every vector has a unique finite linear combination in that basis. Redundant measurements can describe a vector without forming a basis.
glossary.quick_example: In the basis {(1,1),(1,−1)}, the vector (4,2) has coefficients (3,1).
explanation: A basis provides a complete coordinate system with no redundancy. Spanning guarantees that each vector can be represented, while independence guarantees that the coefficients are unique. These are separate requirements; a generating list can span successfully while still storing more measurements than a basis needs.

Choosing a basis also determines the matrices of operators and the coefficient rules for products or derivatives. A different basis can make one operation simpler and another more complicated. In the falling-factorial examples, the basis is chosen to simplify finite differences, so its usefulness comes from the operations being studied rather than from a universally preferred coordinate system.

glossary.definition: The number of vectors in a basis of a finite-dimensional vector space. In these examples, R² has dimension two even when three redundant measurements are stored.
glossary.quick_example: The subspace spanned by (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) has dimension two inside R³.
explanation: Dimension measures the number of independent scalar coordinates needed to specify a vector. It does not count the number of entries in every possible representation. An injective map can store a two-dimensional vector as three measurements, but those three measurements then satisfy a relation.

In finite-dimensional linear problems, dimension helps separate information retained from information lost: rank counts independent output directions, and nullity counts independent erased input directions. It also differs from seed rank, because one seed can generate many independent vectors when nontrivial operators are allowed to act on it.

glossary.definition: For a linear map T, the vectors sent to zero: ker T = {x : Tx = 0}. A nonzero kernel describes directions that this map cannot distinguish from zero.
glossary.example_text: For the sum map R(a,b) = a+b over R, the vector (1,−1)ᵀ lies in the kernel: R(1,−1) = 0. Adding this vector does not change the observed sum.
glossary.quick_example: For R(x,y) = x+y, the kernel is span{(1,−1)}.
explanation: The kernel describes invisible changes to an input. If k lies in ker T, then T(x+k)=Tx for every x, so the map cannot distinguish x from x+k. For a linear map, every nonempty fiber is a translate of this same subspace; one kernel therefore describes all of its ambiguities at once.

This makes kernels central to recovery. A requested linear observation F can be reconstructed from a summary R only when every change erased by R is also erased by F. The condition ker R⊆ker F states that requirement directly. A kernel vector violating it supplies a concrete witness that the summary lost needed information.

glossary.definition: The outputs actually attained by a map. For a linear map T, im T = {Tx : x is an allowed input} is a subspace of the target. The declared target can be larger than the image.
glossary.example_text: For A(a,b) = (a,b,a+b), the image consists of triples whose third coordinate is the sum of the first two. The coordinate vector (0,0,1)ᵀ lies outside it.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,0) has image the horizontal axis, even if its codomain is all of R².
explanation: The image is the set of valid outputs of an operation. In a redundant coordinate system, not every numerical list is valid analyzed data: some lists fail the relations imposed by the analysis map. The image records those consistency requirements as a subspace of the coefficient space.

For example, if A(x,y)=(x,y,x+y), then a triple is in the image exactly when its third entry equals the sum of the first two. A synthesis map may still accept an arbitrary triple, but synthesizing and reanalyzing it can change it into a valid one. That change is a coefficient-space projection, not an identity on all triples.

glossary.definition: For a finite linear map, the dimension of its image. A matrix has full column rank when its columns are linearly independent, so it has no nonzero input in its kernel.
glossary.note: Matrix rank and seed rank answer different questions.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,1],[2,2]] has rank one because its second row and column add no independent direction.
explanation: Rank counts independent output directions, so it measures how many independent linear measurements a map can actually supply. Repeated or linearly dependent rows add storage without increasing rank. Column rank and row rank agree over a field, linking this output-space interpretation to independent measurement rows.

Rank is especially useful when a matrix is rectangular. A map can have full column rank and recover every input while failing to reach its entire codomain. Numerical rank also needs a scale and threshold: a very small computed singular value is not automatically an exact algebraic zero.

glossary.definition: For real vector spaces, a symmetric bilinear pairing with ⟨v,v⟩ > 0 for every nonzero v. It defines lengths and angles. Positive weights give the pairing sum_i w_i u_i v_i. Complex inner products use conjugate symmetry and conjugate linearity in one argument.
glossary.quick_example: For u = (1,2), the weighted inner product with weights (1,3) gives ⟨u,u⟩ = 1+12 = 13.
explanation: An inner product supplies the geometry missing from bare linear algebra. It tells us which directions are perpendicular and gives a norm through ‖v‖²=⟨v,v⟩. Different positive weights change that geometry, so an averaging map can be orthogonal for one weighted pairing and oblique for another.

Over complex scalars, conjugation is essential: without it, the expression for a vector’s squared length need not be positive. Authors choose which argument is conjugate-linear, and adjoint formulas must follow that convention. When a coordinate transformation changes the metric matrix, transpose symmetry in the new coordinates need not describe orthogonality correctly by itself.

glossary.definition: A nonnegative measure of size that is zero only at the zero vector, scales by the absolute value of a scalar and satisfies the triangle inequality. The Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates.
glossary.quick_example: The Euclidean norm of (3,4) is 5, while its 1-norm is 7.
explanation: A norm measures size but does not necessarily specify angles. The triangle inequality makes error bounds possible: the size of a sum of discrepancies is at most the sum of their sizes. Different norms can emphasize different features, such as the largest coordinate, total absolute magnitude or Euclidean energy.

Every reported residual norm should therefore name its convention. The same vector can have several correct numerical sizes under different norms, and an induced operator norm depends on the chosen norms on both input and output. In infinite-dimensional settings, changing the norm can also change which convergence statements are true.

glossary.definition: A system that records which objects an operation accepts and returns. A path of operations is legal only when consecutive input and output types agree. Types are part of the mathematical specification.
explanation: Types prevent formally written operations from being combined when their meanings do not match. A measurement row accepts a state vector and returns a scalar; it cannot generally be followed by a map expecting the original state. The dimensions of finite matrices provide a concrete version of these input and output restrictions.

Typing alone does not establish a system’s equations. Two paths can both be legal yet give different maps. A realization must satisfy the declared relations between legal paths as well as respect their types. This separates a malformed expression from a well-formed expression that fails a proposed mathematical identity.

glossary.definition: In the finite linear setting, a collection of linear operators closed under sums, scalar multiples, and composition. When a unital algebra is intended, the identity operator is included.
explanation: The algebra specifies the allowed linear ways to act: one may compose available operators, add them and scale them. Enlarging this collection can increase what a seed generates without changing the underlying vector space. Thus the action is part of the data in any generator-counting problem.

Composition is generally noncommutative, so reversing two allowed operators can change their result. A unital algebra also includes the empty action through the identity. Infinite-dimensional uses of the phrase may impose topology, norm closure or adjoint closure; the finite algebraic definition here does not automatically include those extra requirements.

glossary.definition: In the finite linear example, the least number of seeds whose operator-generated span is the whole space. More general definitions can involve modules, dense generation, and cardinalities. Read the definition in the chosen work.
glossary.example_text: For N(a,b) = (b,0) on R², one seed v = (0,1) suffices. With only the zero operator and the identity, two seeds are needed on the same space.
explanation: Seed rank measures how many independent starting sources are needed when the operator action does part of the generating work. For a chosen family of seeds, take the span of all their allowed operator images. The family is sufficient when that span equals the required space or satisfies the work’s stated generation condition.

This can be much smaller than vector-space dimension. A cyclic vector gives seed rank one even in a space with many basis directions. Changing the action can change seed rank, and restricting to scalar multiples of the identity returns the usual need for a basis-sized generating family in finite dimensions.

glossary.definition: For a single linear operator T, a vector v is cyclic when v, Tv, T²v and further iterates span the space under consideration. One cyclic vector is enough to generate that operator module.
explanation: A cyclic vector packages enough starting information for repeated application of one operator to generate the whole space by linear combination. In a d-dimensional space, this can be checked by the rank of the d-column matrix [v,Tv,…,Tᵈ⁻¹v]. Later iterates supply no new directions once the generated span becomes invariant.

The vector itself need not visit every vector as an orbit point: linear combinations of orbit points are allowed. Cyclicity also depends on T. A nonzero vector is cyclic for a scalar identity action only in dimension one, whereas suitable nontrivial operators can have cyclic vectors in much larger spaces.

glossary.definition: A projector onto a subspace whose residual x − Px is perpendicular to that subspace in the specified inner product. In ordinary real Euclidean coordinates its matrix is symmetric as well as idempotent.
glossary.note: Orthogonality depends on the inner product. Weighted averaging need not have a symmetric matrix in ordinary coordinates.
glossary.example_text: With weights (1,3,2), the averaging map sends (2,6,9)ᵀ to (5,5,9)ᵀ. Its residual (−3,1,0)ᵀ has weighted inner product −3a + 3a = 0 with every retained vector (a,a,b)ᵀ. The averaging matrix is not symmetric in ordinary coordinates.
explanation: Orthogonal projection keeps the component in the target subspace and leaves a perpendicular residual. This makes the projected point a nearest point in the induced norm in the finite-dimensional setting. It also gives ‖x‖²=‖Px‖²+‖x−Px‖² because the cross term vanishes.

The familiar test P*=P assumes orthonormal coordinates for the stated inner product. With metric matrix G, self-adjointness instead reads P*G=GP. Changing coordinates while retaining an inappropriate Euclidean metric can therefore make a mathematically orthogonal projection appear nonsymmetric or lead to an incorrect energy calculation.

glossary.definition: In these finite examples, projectors Pᵢ with PᵢPⱼ = 0 for distinct indices and sum_i Pᵢ = I. These identities decompose every vector as x = sum_i Pᵢx.
explanation: The sum-to-identity condition guarantees that no component is missing. Mutual annihilation guarantees that the algebraic selections do not overlap in a way that survives applying one projector after another. Together they give a direct-sum decomposition into the packet ranges and recover every input by summing its packet values.

Each condition has its own role. A partial family can remain idempotent and mutually annihilating while failing to reconstruct the whole space. Conversely, arbitrary reconstruction components can sum to the identity without being projectors individually. Completeness of an algebraic packet family also does not establish orthogonality in a chosen metric.

glossary.definition: The relation PᵢPⱼ = 0 whenever i and j differ. Applying one selection after a different selection gives zero. For a pair of projectors, both orders must be checked.
explanation: The relation says that a vector already selected by one projector has zero component under the other selection. It is an algebraic statement about ordered products, rather than a statement about the lengths or angles of the selected vectors. Both products PᵢPⱼ and PⱼPᵢ matter for an unordered pair.

For complete projector families, these zero products make component bookkeeping unambiguous and support reconstruction and block-composition formulas. Orthogonal projectors onto perpendicular subspaces satisfy the relation, but nonorthogonal direct-sum projectors can satisfy it too. The word annihilation here concerns operator composition, not physical destruction of a state.

glossary.definition: A subspace W preserved by an operator T, meaning T(W) is contained in W. Preservation does not require T to act as the identity on W.
explanation: Invariance means that an input starting in W stays in W after the operation, although its value can change substantially there. The restriction of T to W is then an operator on W in its own right. This permits an exact smaller state description for trajectories known to remain in that subspace.

With a projector P onto W, invariance is equivalent to (I−P)TP=0: there is no leakage from retained inputs into discarded outputs. The reverse cross-block can still be nonzero. Invariance of a subspace should therefore be distinguished from a reducing decomposition in which both complementary pieces are preserved.

glossary.definition: A transformation between descriptions of the same object. In the invertible linear example the convention is y = Cx, so x = C⁻¹y. Keeping track of the direction prevents inverse formulas from being swapped.
explanation: The equation y=Cx fixes which direction the coordinate matrix acts. To apply an original operator T to a vector stored as y, first recover x=C⁻¹y, apply T, then convert the output as appropriate. This sequence derives the transported operator rather than relying on a memorized inverse placement.

A coordinate change preserves the represented object but need not preserve ordinary Euclidean lengths of its stored columns. A metric must transform too if geometric quantities are to agree. Rectangular maps between different spaces require separate input and output coordinate changes rather than one common conjugation.

glossary.definition: A map that undoes another map in both directions. For a square invertible matrix C, the inverse satisfies C⁻¹C = CC⁻¹ = I.
explanation: A two-sided inverse establishes a reversible correspondence: neither direction loses information or leaves unreachable target values. For a finite square matrix, checking both products equal I confirms this directly. Over a field, invertibility is equivalent to full rank and a nonzero determinant.

Exact invertibility is separate from stable numerical inversion. A matrix can be invertible while having a very large condition number, so small stored errors can produce large recovered errors. Rectangular analysis maps instead often use a one-sided inverse, whose identity applies only in the relevant composition order.

glossary.definition: For A mapping an input space to a coordinate space, S is a left inverse when SA = I on the input space. This gives exact reconstruction of analyzed inputs. It does not imply AS = I on the entire coordinate space.
glossary.example_text: The redundant-coordinate example has SA = I₂ but AS ≠ I₃. S recovers every original vector even though it does not invert every three-coordinate input.
explanation: The left inverse reconstructs every original input after analysis. It therefore forces A to be injective: if Ax=Ay, applying S gives x=y. Extra coefficient coordinates are allowed, so A can have more rows than columns and still admit exact reconstruction.

There can be many left inverses, differing in how they treat coefficient lists outside im A. Canonical dual synthesis chooses one using the declared inner products. A reconstruction test on valid analyzed data does not determine how a synthesis map should behave on arbitrary inconsistent or noisy coefficient lists.

glossary.definition: A representation containing more coordinate entries than are needed for a basis description. Valid coordinate lists can satisfy relations, such as a third measurement being the sum of the first two.
glossary.note: The reconstruction components SEᵢA can sum to the identity without being projectors.
explanation: Redundancy adds descriptions without adding independent object dimensions. For A(x,y)=(x,y,x+y), the third measurement provides a consistency relation, not a third freely variable object coordinate. Such extra measurements can be useful for checking consistency or distributing reconstruction across several components.

The cost is that coefficient-space identities require care. An arbitrary triple need not be valid analyzed data, and synthesis can have a nonzero kernel of gauge directions. Individual coordinate contributions can sum to the correct object even though none of them is an idempotent packet projector.

glossary.definition: Applying one map after another. In a matrix product UT, T acts first and U acts second. The intermediate dimensions or types must agree.
explanation: Composition connects operations through the actual intermediate object. Its order matters: UT means that T acts first, so its output must be a legal input for U. Associativity permits regrouping compatible operations, but does not permit swapping their order.

If the two stages store the intermediate object in different coordinates, a bridge between those descriptions is required. Omitting it can produce a dimensionally valid matrix product with the wrong meaning. Complete packet decompositions similarly require summing over every relevant intermediate component when composing transfer blocks.

glossary.definition: The change in an operator matrix under an invertible coordinate change. With y = Cx and original operator T, the new matrix is CTC⁻¹. This usage is distinct from complex conjugation.
explanation: Conjugation describes the same endomorphism in a different coordinate system. The rightmost inverse converts the new input coordinates back to the old ones, T performs the original action, and the leftmost C returns the result to the new coordinates.

It preserves algebraic relations: if T²=0, then (CTC⁻¹)²=0, because the intermediate inverse factors cancel. Eigenvalues and minimal polynomial are also preserved. Ordinary transpose symmetry and Euclidean norm values need not be preserved by an arbitrary C, since those depend on metric information as well as linear structure.

glossary.definition: A linear map C connecting operators T and U by CT = UC. Applying T and then C agrees with applying C and then U. An intertwiner need not be invertible.
explanation: The equation CT=UC says that two routes to the target agree: evolve under T and then encode with C, or encode first and evolve under U. Unlike conjugation, this permits C to lose information or embed into a larger space.

If C is a summary map, its kernel must be preserved by T for such an exact reduced evolution to exist on its image. When C is invertible, the equation solves to U=CTC⁻¹. Thus intertwining includes reversible coordinate transport and some irreversible but dynamically compatible summaries.

glossary.definition: Passing to a description that groups or forgets distinctions. Combining fine packets can recover a coarse packet, while discarding the fine values can prevent later reconstruction.
explanation: A coarsening groups fine descriptions into larger classes or discards distinctions between them. Its fibers make the forgotten information explicit: all inputs in one fiber receive the same coarse value. Some requested questions can remain constant on those fibers even when full reconstruction becomes impossible.

For a pair of samples, retaining their average loses the signed difference but still determines their sum. Whether coarsening is acceptable is therefore relative to the task. Applying an operation after coarsening also needs care, because the discarded detail may influence later coarse observations.

glossary.definition: For a sequence x and a positive integer m, the phase r collects samples x_(mk+r), with 0 ≤ r < m. Interleaving all phases reconstructs the indexed sequence. Filtering requires additional boundary and convention choices.
explanation: Polyphase decomposition reorganizes a sequence by its index modulo m. For m=2, one stream contains even-indexed samples and another odd-indexed samples. Keeping all phases with their within-phase positions is reversible; discarding a phase is an additional information-losing operation.

A shift can move a sample to a different phase and also change its within-phase index. That extra carry is why a filter’s polyphase representation is more than a permutation of its scalar taps. Finite signals additionally need a boundary rule before the resulting shifts and filter matrices are determined.

glossary.definition: Integers with the same remainder modulo a positive integer m. Two integers belong to the same class when their difference is a multiple of m. Even and odd indices are the two classes modulo two.
explanation: A residue class is an equivalence class of integer indices, not just the chosen remainder used to label it. The label r usually represents every integer mk+r. Different representatives describe the same class whenever they differ by a multiple of the modulus.

This supplies the address system for polyphase streams and degree selectors. Refining from modulus m to a multiple of m splits each coarse class into finer classes with compatible parent labels. Operations on the actual indices may also change the quotient index k, so the residue label alone does not record the whole shift.

glossary.definition: Agreement between specified maps, operations or levels of a construction. The relevant equality must be stated, such as a coarse projector equaling the sum of its fine children.
explanation: Compatibility says that independently described pieces fit together according to a specified equality. For example, refining and then summing children should agree with selecting the original parent packet. The equality identifies exactly which outputs are meant to coincide and on which inputs.

It is not a general assurance that two constructions are similar or intuitively consistent. A coordinate system, a refinement tower and a dynamics summary each require their own compatibility equations. Checking those equations exposes whether an apparent discrepancy comes from a convention mismatch, omitted data or an actual failure of the proposed construction.

glossary.definition: A diagram in which the declared routes between the same starting and ending objects give the same map. In Example 3 the equality is D_y C = C D.
explanation: A commuting diagram expresses route independence: following either declared path gives the same result at the common endpoint. To read one, identify its starting space, ending space and the composition order along each route, then translate those routes into an equation of maps.

Drawing the diagram does not prove the equation. In a finite linear setting, equality on a spanning family can establish it; for a nonlinear map, sampled agreement generally has narrower scope. A transfer defect quantifies how much the routes disagree when exact commutation is unavailable.

glossary.definition: Recovering an object from its representation under the stated identities. Exact reconstruction may use all packet components or a synthesis map. Dropping components generally introduces a residual.
explanation: Reconstruction asks whether the stored representation determines the object or requested quantity and whether the chosen synthesis rule returns it. An exact identity such as SA=I establishes this for every admissible input in its stated space. A successful single input is only an instance of that identity.

Dropping coordinates changes the reconstruction map and usually introduces a residual. That residual can be computed exactly even when the approximation is poor. Reconstruction accuracy also differs from numerical stability: exact algebraic recovery may amplify small perturbations if the representation is badly conditioned.

glossary.definition: For a map R and an output s, the set of all inputs with R(x) = s. A proposed observation can be recovered from R(x) alone only if it is constant on each fiber.
glossary.example_text: For R(a,b) = a+b on R², the fiber over 1 consists of all (t,1−t) with real t. It contains both (1,0) and (0,1).
explanation: A fiber gathers all inputs that a map regards as indistinguishable at one output value. For a linear summary, each nonempty fiber is a translate of the kernel. For a nonlinear summary, fibers can have very different shapes, sizes or numbers of connected pieces.

Fibers turn a recovery question into a test of constancy. If the requested answer varies within one fiber, the summary cannot determine it. If it is constant on every fiber, an answer rule exists on the attained summary values, although continuity, stable evaluation and efficient computation remain additional questions.

glossary.definition: Writing one map F as G composed with another map R, so F(x) = G(R(x)). This means the intermediate value R(x) contains enough information for the requested output F(x).
explanation: Factoring F through R means that R is an adequate intermediate description for the particular output F. The intermediate rule G uses only R(x), so it cannot consult distinctions already erased by R. The factorization equation must hold throughout the declared input set.

For unrestricted linear maps, ker R⊆ker F supplies the corresponding existence criterion. In the finite matrix setting, one can also seek coefficients expressing the desired measurement rows through the available ones. For nonlinear settings the fiber criterion remains useful even when no kernel or row-space description is available.

glossary.definition: An object at a finer or richer level that maps to a specified object at a coarser level. Existence, uniqueness and compatibility of lifts are separate questions.
explanation: A lift supplies a finer object whose coarse image is the required one. There may be no lift, exactly one lift or many lifts. When many exist, selecting one representative is a further choice and may affect later computations that depend on the hidden finer information.

Across several levels, individually choosing lifts is not enough: their reductions must agree to form a compatible tower. Likewise, finding a lift at every tested finite level does not by itself exhibit one infinite compatible branch. The relevant existence and limit arguments must accompany that stronger claim.

glossary.definition: For positive weights and a finite partition, replace each value by its group’s weighted mean. The resulting map fixes group-constant vectors and is an orthogonal projector in the corresponding weighted inner product.
explanation: In the finite partition model, the operation replaces variation inside each group by a weighted constant. Positive weights determine both the group mean and the inner product in which the residual is perpendicular to group-constant vectors. Applying the averaging again changes nothing, so the map is a projector.

This explains how averaging can preserve all group-constant observations while losing within-group detail. The weights belong to the construction; replacing them can change the means and orthogonality. General measure-theoretic conditional expectation extends the idea but requires its own probability space and integrability hypotheses.

glossary.definition: A construction that adds or realizes limits or missing structure under a specified mathematical definition. There is no single universal completion operation across the collection. A finite compatible tower does not by itself construct an infinite limit.
glossary.note: Mathematical completion and the editorial completion stage of a paper are different uses of the word.
explanation: The meaning of completion depends on what is missing and what equivalence or limiting notion is being used. A metric completion adds limits of suitable Cauchy sequences; an algebraic or realization construction can address a different kind of missing structure. The word alone does not identify one shared operation.

When a work builds compatible finite stages, distinguish the existence of those stages from the existence and properties of a completed object. Additional arguments may be needed for compatibility, convergence, uniqueness or preservation of operations. Editorial labels saying a manuscript is complete concern a separate assessment of its declared scope.

glossary.definition: The capacity of a numerical representation. For the binary model here it is the number of significant binary digits, including the leading bit. More precision does not alone prove that an algorithm or its input is accurate.
explanation: Precision governs how finely a representation can distinguish nearby values at its current scale. For a binary significand with a fixed number of bits, the absolute spacing changes with the exponent. It therefore differs from a fixed decimal error tolerance or the number of trustworthy digits in an answer.

Increasing precision can reduce rounding effects, but cannot repair incorrect formulas, inaccurate input data or omitted approximation terms. It can also expose cancellation or instability that a shorter display concealed. Precision comparisons should distinguish the stored format from the actual error established for the computed quantity.

glossary.definition: A rational number expressible as an integer divided by a power of two. These are precisely the rational numbers with a finite binary expansion, apart from representation range limits.
explanation: A terminating binary fraction is a finite sum of integer multiples of powers of two, which is why its reduced denominator is a power of two. Numbers such as 3/8 fit this pattern, whereas 1/3 does not, despite being an exact rational number.

A dyadic value may still exceed the range or precision of a particular floating-point format. Conversely, a stored binary floating-point number has an exact dyadic interpretation even when it approximates a non-dyadic intended input. Input conversion error and later arithmetic error should therefore be tracked separately.

glossary.definition: Choosing a representable stored value for an exact value according to a specified rule. Nearest, ties to even chooses the closer value and resolves an exact midpoint by the parity of the last retained significand bit.
explanation: Rounding maps an exact value onto the available representable grid. The chosen rule determines which stored neighbor is selected and how midpoint cases are resolved. A rounding error is consequently a property of the exact value, format, scale and rule together.

Repeated rounded operations need not equal one final rounding of the exact combined expression. This matters for cancellation, summation and reproducibility. Directed rounding deliberately selects enclosing neighbors, while nearest rounding aims at closeness; one convention cannot be silently substituted for the other in a numerical certificate.

glossary.definition: A unit in the last retained place at a specified precision and exponent. In the three-bit example the spacing in [1, 2) is 1/4, while the spacing in [2, 4) is 1/2. It is not one fixed absolute distance.
explanation: An ULP expresses spacing in the local representation rather than a universal physical unit. With fixed significand precision, moving to the next exponent interval changes that spacing. Near boundaries, adjacent gaps can differ, so a statement about ULP error must retain the convention being used.

An error measured in a few ULPs can be small relative to a nonzero value’s scale while having very different absolute sizes at different exponents. It should not be confused with a global tolerance. Exceptional values and underflow regions also need the numerical format’s own rules.

glossary.definition: A numerical return whose sign compares the stored result with the exact value under the operation’s contract. Zero means exact, negative means below and positive means above. An error sentinel is not a numerical direction.
explanation: The ternary return records the direction of rounding relative to the exact mathematical result of the specified operation. It is additional information beyond the stored approximation itself. In the stated contract, a negative sign means the stored value is below that exact result, not that the result is negative.

Check the API contract before interpreting a return code. Error indicators, unordered comparisons and numerical direction values can have different roles. The direction also concerns that individual operation and its encoded inputs; it is not a bound on all accumulated error in a longer computation.

glossary.definition: A declared threshold used by a numerical acceptance rule. Its units, scaling and comparison must match the residual being checked. A residual below tolerance is evidence within that rule, not exact equality in general.
explanation: A tolerance defines what a particular acceptance test regards as small enough. Its meaning comes from the tested quantity: an absolute residual, a relative discrepancy, a matrix norm or a probability enclosure can each need a different threshold.

Passing a tolerance test is therefore a scoped numerical statement. A threshold chosen after observing a result can have a different evidential meaning from a justified bound fixed beforehand. Tolerance zero also does not generally convert floating-point calculations into exact proofs; the arithmetic and equality test remain finite representations.

glossary.definition: An assumption required by a statement or construction. It may describe the space, arithmetic, domain, regularity or supplied data. A conclusion applies only where its hypotheses hold.
explanation: Hypotheses delimit the cases in which a statement is asserted. Invertibility, positive weights, a finite domain or a specified coefficient field can each make an otherwise invalid formula correct. Removing one changes the claim rather than merely shortening its presentation.

When applying a theorem, match its hypotheses to the actual problem before using its conclusion. When proposing a counterexample, check that the example satisfies them. A computation can establish some hypotheses for its encoded inputs while leaving others as external mathematical obligations.

glossary.definition: A mathematical statement established by a proof from its specified assumptions. A theorem may be conditional on explicit hypotheses, even when the implication itself is fully proved.
explanation: A theorem is a proved statement with a particular logical scope. It can assert an implication, an existence result, an equivalence or a bound, and these forms have different uses. For example, an existence theorem need not provide an efficient construction of the object whose existence it proves.

The theorem’s assumptions, definitions and dependencies travel with its conclusion. A finite example can illustrate it, and a formal companion can cover a precisely encoded version, but neither automatically enlarges the written result. Distinguishing mathematical validity from implementation efficiency is especially important in computational applications.

glossary.definition: An argument establishing a statement from its hypotheses and accepted prior results. A worked input illustrates a statement. A general identity or argument is needed to establish a claim about every allowed input.
explanation: A proof explains why the conclusion follows throughout the stated domain. Its steps can use definitions, logical inference, algebraic identities and established results. A chain of correct calculations still needs to address the actual hypotheses and quantifiers of the claim being proved.

Examples are valuable for understanding and detecting errors, but sampled agreement does not generally settle a universal statement. Exhaustive checking of a finite domain can form a proof when coverage and checking correctness are established. Formal verification likewise proves the encoded proposition, whose correspondence with the intended written claim needs separate care.

glossary.definition: A method for discovery, search or estimation without a complete guarantee for the claimed outcome. Its suggestions can lead to later proofs or checks, but the suggestions alone do not establish them.
explanation: A heuristic can guide which seed, candidate, parameter or proof route to investigate next. Its value may come from producing useful suggestions quickly, even when it cannot guarantee success or optimality. The suggestion and its later verification are different stages.

A failed heuristic search does not establish that no solution exists. A successful heuristic proposal can become rigorous evidence after an appropriate exact or validated check. Claims about reliability or performance should describe the tested population and resource limits rather than turn favorable examples into an unrestricted guarantee.

glossary.definition: A check over specified, finitely many inputs or cases. Exhaustive checking can prove a claim about that finite domain. Sampling a larger domain does not establish the universal claim without an additional argument.
explanation: A finite check has a declared population of cases. It can be exhaustive over that population or sample only some of it. These alternatives must be distinguished because checking every member of a finite domain can settle a finite claim, while testing a subset leaves untested cases.

Coverage is part of the evidence: bounds, skipped cases, early exits and resource caps matter. An exact computation removes rounding concerns for the arithmetic performed, but does not automatically prove that the enumerator covered the promised population or that a finite pattern continues indefinitely.

glossary.definition: A subset of a vector space that contains zero and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Kernels and images of linear maps are subspaces.
glossary.quick_example: The plane z = 0 in R³ is a subspace; the parallel plane z = 1 is not.
explanation: A subspace is a smaller linear world inside a larger one: the inherited addition and scaling operations still work without leaving it. Homogeneous linear equations define subspaces because combining two solutions produces another solution. Equations with a nonzero offset generally define affine sets instead.

Subspaces can play different roles in a calculation. A kernel describes erased directions, an image describes attainable outputs, and an invariant subspace describes directions preserved by an evolution. Those roles should be checked separately; being a subspace alone says nothing about whether an operator preserves or projects onto it.

glossary.definition: The dimension of the kernel of a finite-dimensional linear map. It counts independent input directions erased by the map.
glossary.example_text: For T(x₁,x₂,x₃) = (x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃), the kernel is span{(−1,1,−1)ᵀ}. It has one free direction, so nullity T = 1.
glossary.quick_example: The map R(x,y,z) = x+y has kernel {(a,−a,b)}, so its nullity is two.
explanation: Nullity measures how many independent degrees of freedom the map completely erases. If two inputs differ by a kernel vector, they give the same output, so a nullity greater than zero means that unrestricted input recovery is impossible. It does not say that every requested observation is unrecoverable.

For a matrix with n columns, nullity is n minus its rank. This formula refers to the input dimension, not to the number of output rows. Adding dependent output measurements can enlarge the stored result while leaving both rank and nullity unchanged, which is why extra coordinates need not supply extra information.

glossary.definition: For a linear map with finite-dimensional domain V, dim V = rank T + nullity T. The rank concerns the image, not the dimension of the entire declared target.
glossary.example_text: The map T(x₁,x₂,x₃) = (x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃) has rank two and a one-dimensional kernel. Its three-dimensional domain therefore satisfies 3 = 2 + 1 = rank T + nullity T.
glossary.quick_example: For R(x,y,z) = x+y, domain dimension 3 equals rank 1 plus nullity 2.
explanation: The identity divides the finite input dimension into two parts: directions visible in the image and directions invisible in the kernel. One way to understand it is to begin with a basis of the kernel and extend that to a basis of the domain; the added basis vectors supply independent output directions.

This count is a bookkeeping identity for a specified linear map. It does not identify the kernel directions, construct a recovery map or establish good numerical conditioning. Those require additional information. In particular, a full-rank matrix can still amplify small input errors severely when it is close to losing rank.

glossary.definition: A map that sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel contains only zero.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,2x) is injective, although it does not reach every pair.
explanation: Injectivity means that an output identifies at most one input. For a linear map, any collision Tx=Ty is equivalent to T(x−y)=0, which explains the kernel criterion. An injective analysis map therefore retains enough information for a left inverse on its image.

This says nothing about whether every vector in the declared codomain is attained. Redundant measurements often use an injective map into a larger coefficient space, with only a proper subspace consisting of valid measurements. Nor does injectivity guarantee a numerically stable inverse; conditioning controls how accurately that retained information can be recovered.

glossary.definition: A map whose image is its entire declared target. Surjectivity depends on which target is specified.
glossary.quick_example: The map (x,y) ↦ x reaches every real number, although many pairs have the same output.
explanation: Surjectivity means that every requested target value is attainable by some input. It is therefore a statement about both the rule and its declared codomain. The same rule may be surjective when its target is its image and nonsurjective when a larger target is declared.

An output can have many preimages even when the map is surjective. Choosing one preimage for each output gives a right inverse when such a choice is available, but generally does not recover an arbitrary original input. In linear recovery problems, the kernel describes the freedom among those possible preimages.

glossary.definition: A bijective linear map between vector spaces over the same field. Its inverse is linear. It preserves the vector-space structure, although lengths need not be preserved.
explanation: A linear isomorphism lets us regard two vector spaces as equivalent descriptions of the same linear structure. Both the forward map and its inverse preserve linear combinations. In finite dimensions, an invertible square coordinate matrix provides such an equivalence between coordinate descriptions.

Additional structure needs additional preservation requirements. A linear isomorphism can stretch lengths, fail to preserve a chosen multiplication or change the appearance of an inner product. Accordingly, a vector-space isomorphism is not automatically an isometry or an algebra isomorphism. The collection’s transported-product examples make this distinction concrete.

glossary.definition: A decomposition into subspaces in which each vector has a unique sum of components. For two subspaces, uniqueness is equivalent to their intersection containing only zero.
glossary.quick_example: Every pair (x,y) is uniquely (x,0)+(0,y), the sum of one vector from each coordinate axis.
explanation: The uniqueness of the component decomposition is the important extra condition. Merely saying that two subspaces span a space allows overlaps and ambiguous components. For an internal direct sum of two subspaces, every vector splits into one vector from each, and their intersection contains only zero.

Orthogonality is a stronger geometric requirement, not part of the algebraic direct-sum definition. Complementary subspaces can meet at an oblique angle. Their associated projectors still reconstruct each vector, but squared lengths of the components need not add to the original squared length without cross terms.

glossary.definition: The vector space V/W obtained by identifying vectors whose difference lies in a subspace W. A coset x+W records the equivalence class of x.
glossary.quick_example: Modulo span{(1,−1)}, the pairs (2,3) and (4,1) represent the same class because their difference is (2,−2).
explanation: A quotient keeps an equivalence class rather than a particular representative. Writing x+W means that adding any vector of W makes no difference to the retained description. Addition and scaling of classes are well defined because W is a subspace, so different representatives produce the same resulting class.

For a linear summary R, quotienting its domain by ker R removes exactly the distinctions R forgets. The resulting quotient is naturally isomorphic to im R. Recovering another linear observation from that summary therefore asks whether the observation also ignores those discarded directions, rather than whether a preferred representative can be guessed.

glossary.definition: A nonzero vector v for which Tv = λv. The scalar λ is the associated eigenvalue. Zero is excluded from the definition of eigenvector.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,3), the nonzero vector (1,0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.
explanation: An eigenvector identifies a direction on which the operator acts by one scalar. The vector may grow, shrink, reverse sign or rotate in complex phase according to its eigenvalue, but no new direction appears in that one-dimensional subspace. Every nonzero scalar multiple of the eigenvector has the same property.

An eigenvector is always nonzero; allowing zero would make every scalar appear to be an eigenvalue. A single eigenvector also need not describe the operator’s behavior on other inputs. Building an entire basis of eigenvectors is the stronger diagonalizability condition, and some operators do not have such a basis.

glossary.definition: A scalar λ such that Tv = λv for some nonzero v over the specified field. A real matrix may have no real eigenvalue even though it has eigenvalues over the complex numbers.
explanation: Eigenvalues reveal scalar behavior on invariant directions. Repeated powers multiply an eigenvector by λⁿ, which makes them useful for studying iteration. They depend on the coefficient field: a quarter-turn matrix has complex eigenvalues i and −i but no real eigenvector direction.

Eigenvalues alone can miss large one-step or transient amplification in a nonnormal matrix. They also do not describe the gain of a rectangular map, for which singular values are more appropriate. A spectral claim should state the field, multiplicities and structural assumptions under which eigenvalue information is being used.

glossary.definition: For an operator T and scalar λ, the kernel of T − λI. It includes zero and all eigenvectors with eigenvalue λ.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,2,3), the eigenvalue-2 eigenspace is the plane {(x,y,0)}.
explanation: The eigenspace gathers all vectors on which T acts as multiplication by the same λ, including zero so that the collection forms a subspace. It is obtained by solving the homogeneous equation (T−λI)v=0. Its dimension counts independent eigenvector directions for that eigenvalue.

That dimension need not equal the multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial. A defective operator can have too few eigenvectors even when its eigenvalues are known exactly. Spectral projectors onto ordinary eigenspaces therefore need the diagonalizable setting used in the introductory example or a more general spectral construction.

glossary.definition: An operator that has a basis of eigenvectors over the stated field. Equivalently, its matrix becomes diagonal after an invertible change of basis.
explanation: An eigenbasis changes a coupled operation into independent scalar actions: in those coordinates T becomes a diagonal matrix. Applying a polynomial or a repeated power then amounts to applying the corresponding scalar function to each diagonal entry. This is an exact algebraic simplification of the operator.

The eigenbasis need not be orthonormal or well conditioned. A diagonalizable matrix can still have large coordinate amplification when the basis change is poorly conditioned. Normal complex matrices provide the stronger orthonormal-eigenbasis situation; a nonzero nilpotent matrix provides a simple example that is not diagonalizable at all.

glossary.definition: Substitute T into p(t) = a₀ + a₁t + ⋯ + aₙtⁿ to obtain p(T) = a₀I + a₁T + ⋯ + aₙTⁿ. The constant term acts through the identity operator.
explanation: Operator powers mean repeated composition, so p(T) combines several iteration lengths of the same operation. The constant coefficient multiplies I rather than every matrix entry. This convention makes polynomial identities transferable from scalar polynomials to their evaluations at one fixed operator.

For a nilpotent N with N²=0, all terms involving N² or higher vanish, so every polynomial in N reduces to a₀I+a₁N. In spectral examples, interpolation polynomials can select eigenspaces. These calculations concern one operator; substituting several noncommuting operators into a multivariable expression requires an ordering convention.

glossary.definition: For a linear operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional space over a field, the monic polynomial of least degree with m(T) = 0. It records an exact operator relation.
glossary.quick_example: For T = diag(2,3), the minimal polynomial is (t−2)(t−3).
explanation: The minimal polynomial is the shortest monic polynomial relation satisfied by the entire operator. If m has degree d, its equation expresses Tᵈ as a linear combination of lower powers. Higher powers can consequently be reduced using the same relation, which is useful in exact operator calculations.

It must annihilate every input, unlike a relation satisfied only by the orbit of one particular vector. It also differs from the characteristic polynomial, although the latter is an annihilating polynomial by Cayley–Hamilton. Repeated factors in the minimal polynomial record structure that an eigenvalue list alone can miss.

glossary.definition: In the diagonalizable finite example, the projector onto one eigenspace along the sum of the others. Distinct eigenvalues allow a polynomial interpolation formula for these projectors.
glossary.example_text: For T(a,b) = (2a+b,3b), the projectors P₂ = 3I−T and P₃ = T−2I split (2,3)ᵀ into (−1,0)ᵀ and (3,3)ᵀ. The identity T = 2P₂+3P₃ then gives T(2,3)ᵀ = (7,9)ᵀ.
explanation: In the finite diagonalizable setting, a polynomial can be chosen to equal one at a selected eigenvalue and zero at all the others. Evaluating it at T gives the corresponding eigenspace projector. For distinct eigenvalues λⱼ, its factors divide by differences λᵢ−λⱼ, so distinctness is essential to this formula.

These projectors sum to the identity and reconstruct both vectors and the operator through its spectral components. They need not be orthogonal when the eigenbasis is oblique. Nondiagonalizable operators require additional generalized-eigenspace structure; simply reusing the elementary interpolation formula can omit part of the operator.

glossary.definition: For operators on the same space, [A,B] = AB − BA. A zero commutator means the two orders of composition agree.
glossary.quick_example: For P = diag(1,0) and T swapping coordinates, PT−TP = [[0,1],[−1,0]].
explanation: The commutator isolates the failure of two operations to be interchangeable. Applied to x, it compares the actual outputs ABx and BAx in the same space. A nonzero result for even one input disproves commutation, while proving the operator commutator zero establishes agreement on every input.

This is useful for filtering versus coarsening, changing coordinates versus applying an operation, and raising versus lowering degree. A commutator identity can itself encode structure, such as ΔA−AΔ=I on polynomials. Finite truncations may introduce boundary terms, so an identity on the full space need not survive dropping the highest coordinate.

glossary.definition: A matrix grouped into rectangular submatrices according to decompositions of its input and output coordinates. Block products require the inner dimensions to agree.
explanation: Blocks group related coordinates so that a large linear map can be read as interactions between spaces. A block row collects contributions to one output group, while a block column follows the outputs caused by one input group. The blocks can be rectangular and have different sizes.

Block multiplication sums over the shared intermediate groups, exactly as ordinary matrix multiplication sums over coordinates. Writing a matrix in blocks is initially just bookkeeping; treating some blocks as zero, diagonal or invertible is an additional mathematical assumption that must be justified.

glossary.definition: For the block matrix [[A,B],[C,D]] with invertible A, the Schur complement of A is D − CA⁻¹B. It is the remaining operator after eliminating the first block of unknowns.
glossary.quick_example: In [[2,1],[1,3]], eliminating the invertible upper-left entry gives the scalar complement 3−1/2 = 5/2.
