explanation: In the system Au+Bv=f and Cu+Dv=g, solving the first equation gives u=A⁻¹(f−Bv). Substitution into the second leaves (D−CA⁻¹B)v=g−CA⁻¹f. The Schur complement is therefore the effective remaining operator after accounting for the eliminated variables.

The inverse of A is essential to this elementary formula. A singular positive-semidefinite block requires a separate range condition before a pseudoinverse formula can replace it. Ignoring that condition can make an infeasible augmented matrix appear acceptable from the scalar inequality alone.

glossary.definition: Removing selected unknowns by solving part of a system and substituting into the remaining equations. The substitution requires its stated invertibility or solvability assumptions.
explanation: Elimination moves the influence of removed unknowns into a remaining equation; it does not simply delete their rows and columns. Solving a block and substituting it back preserves the original system only under the required solvability conditions and with the substituted right-hand side retained.

The resulting reduced operator often contains new interactions, such as a Schur-complement correction. Singular blocks can leave compatibility constraints or free variables. Any reduction that silently assumes a unique solution for such a block can change the set of admissible original solutions.

glossary.definition: A scalar attached to a square matrix. For [[a,b],[c,d]] it is ad − bc. Over a field, a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,2],[3,4]] has determinant 4−6 = −2 and is invertible over the real numbers.
explanation: The determinant detects invertibility of a square linear coordinate map over a field. Geometrically over the reals, its absolute value is the volume-scaling factor, while its sign records orientation. A zero determinant means that some independent input directions have collapsed into dependence.

Its numerical magnitude is not a general conditioning measure: it mixes the scales of all directions through a product. A diagonal matrix can have determinant one while stretching one direction enormously and shrinking another. Rectangular matrices also need rank or singular-value information rather than a determinant test.

glossary.definition: The relation a ≡ b modulo m means m divides a − b, with m a positive integer. It compares residue classes, not the ordinary sizes of a and b.
glossary.quick_example: 17 and 2 are congruent modulo 5 because their difference 15 is divisible by 5.
explanation: Congruence retains divisibility information while forgetting which integer representative was chosen. If a≡b modulo m, adding the same integer or multiplying by the same integer preserves the relation. This makes residue classes a consistent arithmetic system.

Division is more restrictive. Cancelling a factor modulo m requires appropriate invertibility, so ordinary-looking algebraic manipulations can fail when that factor shares a divisor with m. The modulus belongs with every modular statement, especially when comparing lift branches or combining several residue conditions.

glossary.definition: Integers with greatest common divisor one. Pairwise coprime moduli give independent residue coordinates in the ordinary Chinese remainder theorem.
glossary.quick_example: The integers 4 and 9 are coprime; 4 and 6 have common divisor 2.
explanation: Coprimality means that two integers share no prime factor. Bézout’s identity expresses this as an integer combination au+bv=1, which explains both modular inverses and the independence of residue coordinates in the elementary Chinese remainder theorem.

For several moduli, pairwise coprime means every distinct pair has gcd one; this is stronger than saying that the gcd of the whole list is one. If moduli share factors, compatible residues can still sometimes be combined, but the ordinary product-modulus uniqueness statement needs modification.

glossary.definition: An integer b with ab ≡ 1 modulo m. For m greater than one, it exists exactly when a and m are coprime. The inverse is a residue class modulo m.
glossary.quick_example: The inverse of 3 modulo 7 is 5 because 3·5 = 15 is congruent to 1.
explanation: A modular inverse undoes multiplication within residue classes. If ab≡1 modulo m, multiplying by b reverses the effect of multiplying by a modulo m. Different integer representatives of b describe the same inverse class.

Existence is controlled by gcd(a,m)=1. A nonzero residue need not be invertible when the modulus is composite: 2 modulo 6 is an example. This is why prime fields behave differently from general modular rings and why divisions in roots-of-unity or interpolation formulas require explicit denominator checks.

glossary.definition: For pairwise coprime positive moduli, a tuple of residues specifies exactly one residue class modulo their product. Selecting an integer representative requires an additional convention.
glossary.quick_example: The requirements x ≡ 1 modulo 2 and x ≡ 2 modulo 3 give x ≡ 5 modulo 6.
explanation: The theorem combines several compatible pieces of modular information into one class when the moduli are pairwise coprime. The product modulus is the combined period: adding that product changes none of the individual residues.

It determines a class, not a unique ordinary integer, until a representative interval or another convention is fixed. Shared factors between moduli introduce compatibility requirements and change the combined modulus. In reconstruction problems, keep the modular solution separate from any later claim about bounded integer recovery or an infinite lift.

glossary.definition: A two-sample transform that separates an average and a difference. The tutorial uses a = (u+v)/2 and d = (u−v)/2, with inverse (u,v) = (a+d,a−d). Other Haar normalizations use square roots.
explanation: The average records the common level of two samples, while the detail records how they differ. Together they contain exactly the original two numbers because adding and subtracting the stored values recovers u and v. Retaining only the average merges many distinct input pairs.

The tutorial’s half-sum and half-difference convention is convenient for averaging, but its energy identity has a factor of two. Orthonormal Haar coordinates use a different scaling. Both are legitimate transforms; the inverse and coefficient weights must match whichever normalization is chosen.

glossary.definition: In the Haar pair example, the signed half-difference d = (u−v)/2. It records the information lost when the pair is replaced by its repeated average.
explanation: The sign of the detail tells which sample is larger, and its magnitude measures their contrast under the chosen scaling. Adding it to the average restores one sample; subtracting it restores the other. It therefore carries exactly the information the repeated average omits in a two-sample Haar split.

At multiple scales, details describe differences at their own resolutions. Their numerical magnitudes cannot automatically be compared as equal energy contributions, because normalization and scale weights matter. Dropping selected details produces an explicit reconstruction residual rather than merely changing an index label.

glossary.definition: A real square matrix Q with QᵀQ = QQᵀ = I. It preserves the Euclidean inner product and norm. A transform with orthogonal rows can still need normalization to satisfy this identity.
explanation: The transpose undoes an orthogonal coordinate transformation because the columns form an orthonormal basis. Consequently dot products and Euclidean norms are unchanged. Rotations and reflections provide familiar examples; a determinant of either +1 or −1 is possible.

Mutually perpendicular rows are insufficient unless their lengths are normalized appropriately. The sum-and-difference Haar matrix, for example, needs a scaling choice before it becomes orthogonal. For complex matrices the corresponding condition uses conjugate transpose and is called unitarity.

glossary.definition: A declared scaling convention. For a Haar pair, dividing sums and differences by two gives averages, while dividing by √2 gives a Euclidean norm-preserving transform.
explanation: Normalization fixes the scale at which coordinates, transforms or probabilities are reported. Two formulas can describe equivalent information while using different numerical coefficients. The inverse map, coefficient metric and error thresholds must follow the same convention for their results to agree.

In a Haar pair, average/detail scaling gives u²+v²=2(a²+d²), whereas orthonormal scaling removes that factor. In a Fourier transform, the factor 1/N may be placed in the inverse or split between directions. A comparison made before matching these conventions can mistake a predictable scale factor for an error.

glossary.definition: A sequence of arrows in which each output type matches the next input type. Its realization is the corresponding ordered composition. An empty path at a type acts as its identity.
explanation: A typed path records a legal chain of operations, including its starting and ending types. Its realized matrix product is read from right to left when column-vector conventions are used. The intermediate types explain which matrices are being multiplied rather than merely supplying a dimensional coincidence.

Different paths can have the same endpoints without being equivalent. A declared relation may identify their composites, and a realization must respect that relation. The empty path supplies the identity at its own type, allowing paths of length zero to participate consistently in composition and algebraic equations.

glossary.definition: A required equality between legal operator expressions, such as T² = 0. In a typed system, both sides must have the same input and output types.
explanation: A relation is an equation that the allowed operations are required to satisfy. It can describe nilpotence, commutation, reconstruction or a more complicated equality of paths. Its significance is universal within the stated model: both sides act identically on every admissible input of their common type.

Testing a few vectors can suggest a relation but does not generally prove it. In a finite linear space, checking a spanning family can suffice because linearity extends the equality to every vector. A proposed realization is valid only when all required relations hold, not just when its maps have the correct sizes.

glossary.definition: The declared input and target spaces of a map. The codomain includes all permitted outputs, while the image consists of outputs actually attained.
glossary.quick_example: For T: R² → R³ with T(x,y) = (x,y,0), the domain is R², codomain is R³ and image is a plane.
explanation: The domain tells us which inputs a formula is required to handle; the codomain tells us where its outputs are declared to live. This information determines whether compositions are legal and what claims such as surjectivity mean. The actual image is obtained only after examining the rule.

Restrictions can materially change a problem. A summary that loses information on all of R² might become injective on a specified line. Conversely, a formula that works on valid analyzed coordinates may fail on arbitrary coefficient lists. Recovery and transfer claims should therefore state their admissible input set as well as their map formulas.

glossary.definition: The scalar multiplying a specified basis term. In f(z) = sum aₙzⁿ, aₙ is the coefficient of zⁿ.
glossary.quick_example: In 2+5x+3x², the coefficient of x is 5; in a different basis the coefficient list changes.
explanation: A coefficient is attached to a particular basis element, not just to the represented object. The same polynomial can have different coefficient lists in ordinary powers and falling factorials. Specifying the basis is therefore part of specifying which scalar is being read.

Normalization matters too. In an exponential generating function, the stored sequence entry multiplies tⁿ/n!, so the ordinary coefficient of tⁿ is smaller by n!. Changing basis or normalization without changing coefficient formulas can create incorrect products, derivatives and comparisons.

glossary.definition: An expression sum aₙzⁿ with infinitely many coefficient positions. A formal power series is manipulated through its coefficients. Evaluating it at a number additionally requires convergence.
explanation: A power series stores one coefficient at each nonnegative degree. Its formal interpretation supports algebraic manipulation degree by degree: only finitely many terms contribute to a fixed product coefficient. No numerical value of the variable needs to be chosen for those identities.

To interpret the same expression as a function, establish where the series converges and which operations are justified there. A finite list of coefficients does not determine the size of the omitted tail without further information. This is why truncation identities and analytic error bounds are recorded separately.

glossary.definition: Keeping only specified degrees or levels. Equality modulo zᴺ means the coefficients of degrees below N agree. It need not be equality of the full functions or series.
explanation: Truncation produces a finite description by discarding selected positions. Equality modulo zᴺ checks all coefficients of degrees 0 through N−1 while deliberately leaving higher degrees unspecified. Two very different full series can agree to that finite order.

The discarded part must be controlled separately when evaluating a function or applying an operation that moves information across the truncation boundary. Raising polynomial degree, for example, can require an extra intermediate coordinate. Simply dropping that coordinate can change an otherwise exact operator identity.

glossary.definition: For a power series over a field with nonzero constant coefficient, the unique series whose product with it is one. Its coefficients are determined recursively. A finite truncation only verifies the corresponding finite set of coefficient identities.
aliases: Multiplicative inverse of a formal series
glossary.quick_example: The formal reciprocal of 1−z is 1+z+z²+⋯ because their Cauchy product is 1.
explanation: Multiplying A(z) by its reciprocal B(z) and equating coefficients determines B successively. The constant equation fixes b₀=1/a₀; each later equation contains the new bₙ multiplied by a₀ and terms already known. This explains the nonzero-constant-term requirement over a field.

The inverse concerns multiplication, so it differs from a substitution inverse. Computing the first N coefficients establishes A(z)B(z)=1 modulo zᴺ, not a complete analytic statement about values at every z. Convergence and evaluation errors need their own arguments.

glossary.definition: The multiplication rule cₙ = sum from k=0 to n of aₖbₙ₋ₖ for ordinary power series. Each output coefficient is a finite sum, even when the series are infinite.
explanation: Convolution collects all degree pairs that contribute to one output degree. To form degree n, combine the degree-k term of one factor with the degree-(n−k) term of the other and sum over k. This is why each coefficient uses finitely many terms even for infinite formal series.

The coefficient convention determines the weights. Ordinary powers give this unweighted sum, while factorially normalized exponential series produce binomial coefficients. Signal convolution is related but also requires an index direction and boundary convention when the stored signal is finite.

glossary.definition: A complex number ω with ωᴺ = 1 for a positive integer N. It is primitive when N is its least positive such exponent. A weighted average over the powers of a primitive Nth root selects coefficients in one residue class modulo N.
glossary.quick_example: The number i has exact order 4: i⁴ = 1, and no smaller positive power equals 1.
explanation: Powers of a root of unity describe a finite cyclic phase action. Primitive order means that the complete cycle has the claimed length; a root whose true order divides N visits fewer distinct phases. This distinction is essential for exact averaging and cyclic reachability arguments.

The weighted phase sum cancels monomials in unwanted residue classes and retains those in the selected class. Over other fields, the required root and division by the cycle length may be unavailable. The coefficient selector can still exist algebraically even when this particular averaging realization does not.

glossary.definition: For real a and b, the conjugate of a+bi is a−bi. The squared modulus is (a+bi)(a−bi) = a²+b².
explanation: Conjugation reverses the imaginary part while leaving the real part unchanged. Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate produces its nonnegative squared modulus, which explains why conjugation appears in complex lengths and quantum probabilities.

Conjugating a product conjugates each factor without reversing their scalar order. For matrices, the adjoint additionally transposes the entries and reverses the order of a matrix product. Operator conjugation CTC⁻¹ is a different construction despite sharing the word conjugation.

glossary.definition: For a complex matrix in orthonormal bases, the adjoint A* is its conjugate transpose. In real orthonormal bases this is the ordinary transpose.
glossary.quick_example: The adjoint of [[1,i],[0,2]] is [[1,0],[−i,2]]. Both transposition and conjugation are required.
explanation: The adjoint is characterized by moving an operator across an inner-product pairing. In orthonormal complex coordinates this produces conjugate transpose, so both the entry positions and their imaginary signs change. For products, (AB)*=B*A*, with reversed order.

The coordinate formula depends on the inner products. With nonidentity metric matrices, raw conjugate transpose no longer represents the same adjoint operation without metric factors. This matters when comparing unitary or self-adjoint operators across nonorthonormal coordinate systems.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix U with U*U = UU* = I. It preserves the complex inner product and therefore vector norms.
glossary.quick_example: diag(1,i) is unitary because its adjoint diag(1,−i) is its inverse.
explanation: A unitary map is a reversible complex linear change preserving the inner product. Its adjoint supplies its inverse, so it preserves normalization and all pairwise geometric relations between state vectors.

In density-matrix form it acts by ρ↦UρU*, preserving eigenvalues and purity. This differs from a general quantum channel, which can discard information or turn a pure state into a mixed one. Unitarity also does not mean that probabilities in a fixed measurement basis remain unchanged; the state’s coordinates can rotate.

glossary.definition: A complex coordinate of a normalized state vector in a chosen orthonormal basis. Its squared modulus gives that basis outcome’s probability. Relative phases can affect measurements in other bases.
explanation: An amplitude has both magnitude and phase. Squaring its modulus gives a probability only after a normalized state and an orthonormal measurement basis have been specified. Individual amplitudes can interfere when the measurement basis changes.

Consequently, keeping only their squared magnitudes loses information about relative phase. The demonstration’s states with phases 1 and −1 have identical coordinate probabilities but different X-measurement probabilities. This distinguishes a state vector’s full information from the probability list of one particular measurement.

glossary.definition: A positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. A normalized vector ψ gives the pure-state matrix ρ = ψψ*. Different vectors that differ only by an overall complex phase give the same density matrix.
glossary.example_text: The normalized vector ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ gives ρ = ψψ*. Its diagonal entries are 9/25 and 16/25, its upper-right entry is −12i/25, and its lower-left entry is 12i/25. Its trace is one.
explanation: A density matrix describes a state in a way that supports both pure states and mixtures. Its trace-one condition normalizes total probability, while positive semidefiniteness ensures that every valid measurement effect has a nonnegative probability.

For a pure state, the outer product removes the unobservable common phase while retaining relative phases in off-diagonal entries. A mixed density matrix can have several different ensemble decompositions, so it does not identify a unique hidden list of prepared pure states. Measurements determine the matrix’s observable consequences.

glossary.definition: The sum of diagonal entries of a square matrix. It is unchanged by an invertible change of basis. Field trace is a related arithmetic construction with its own definition.
explanation: Trace adds the diagonal contributions of an endomorphism and is independent of the basis used to represent that endomorphism. Compatible finite matrix products satisfy tr(AB)=tr(BA), which often simplifies probability and channel-normalization calculations.

It is a scalar summary and does not determine the matrix. Many different density matrices share trace one. Positivity must therefore be checked separately; a Hermitian trace-one matrix with a negative eigenvalue is not a valid quantum state.

glossary.definition: For a density matrix ρ and an orthogonal measurement projector P, the outcome probability is tr(Pρ). A complete orthogonal projector family gives probabilities summing to one.
glossary.example_text: For ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ and ρ = ψψ*, the coordinate projectors P₀ = diag(1,0) and P₁ = diag(0,1) give tr(P₀ρ) = 9/25 and tr(P₁ρ) = 16/25. These probabilities sum to one.
explanation: The Born rule pairs a state with a specified measurement outcome. For projective measurements, the trace formula agrees with the squared norm of the projected pure-state vector. Completeness of the measurement projectors makes the total probability one.

Changing the measurement changes the question being asked of the same state. Coordinate probabilities may ignore coherences that another basis can detect. General measurements use positive effects summing to I, while the projective form in this entry is the important special case used in the introductory example.

glossary.definition: The number tr(ρ²). For a finite density matrix it equals one exactly for a pure state and is smaller for a mixed state.
glossary.example_text: For ρ = ψψ* with ψ = (3/5,4i/5)ᵀ, tr(ρ²) = 1. After coordinate dephasing, the purity is (9/25)² + (16/25)² = 337/625, which is less than one.
explanation: Purity depends on the eigenvalues of the density matrix: it is their squared sum. A pure state concentrates the whole trace in one eigenvalue equal to one. For a d-dimensional state, the completely mixed matrix I/d has purity 1/d.

Unitary coordinate changes preserve purity, whereas dephasing can reduce it by removing off-diagonal coherence. Purity is still only one scalar and does not determine the state or its measurement probabilities. Compare it together with the density matrix and the operation that produced it.

glossary.definition: For a specified complete orthogonal family Pᵢ, the channel ρ ↦ sum PᵢρPᵢ removes coherence between different selected subspaces. Its effect depends on the chosen decomposition.
glossary.example_text: The coordinate measurement with its outcome forgotten sends the example’s ρ to P₀ρP₀ + P₁ρP₁ = diag(9/25,16/25). The off-diagonal terms disappear while the two coordinate probabilities remain unchanged.
explanation: Dephasing keeps the diagonal packet blocks PᵢρPᵢ and deletes the cross-blocks PᵢρPⱼ for different indices. It models a projective measurement whose outcome has been discarded. Applying the same complete dephasing again makes no further change.

The retained information depends on the chosen decomposition. Coherences inside a multidimensional retained block can remain, while coherences between blocks vanish. Diagonal observations can stay exactly recoverable even when other measurement probabilities cannot be recovered from the dephased output alone.

glossary.definition: Matrices Kᵢ describing a finite quantum channel by Φ(ρ) = sum KᵢρKᵢ*. The condition sum Kᵢ*Kᵢ = I makes this map trace preserving.
explanation: Each Kraus term contributes one possible branch to a channel’s unconditioned output. Summing the terms gives a completely positive map, and the completeness equation makes the trace of every input state remain one.

The Kraus representation is generally not unique, so its individual matrices are not automatically unique physical events. If a branch is interpreted as a measured outcome, its probability and conditional normalization must be specified. A complete channel and one selected branch therefore have different trace and information interpretations.

glossary.definition: An integer pⁿ with p prime and n a nonnegative integer. Successive positive powers give the moduli in the lift-branch example.
explanation: Powers of one prime provide nested modular resolutions. Moving from pⁿ to pⁿ⁺¹ retains the old residue information while allowing one additional base-p digit. The primality assumption gives the arithmetic structure used in p-adic lifting arguments.

Level zero corresponds to p⁰=1, whose residue information is trivial. A solution modulo one prime power need not extend to every higher power. The lifting equations and compatibility maps determine which next digits are allowed.

glossary.definition: Passing from a residue class modulo pⁿ⁺¹ to its class modulo pⁿ. This map forgets the highest retained base-p digit.
explanation: Reduction preserves the lower-level residue while forgetting finer digits. Several residues modulo pⁿ⁺¹ therefore share one image modulo pⁿ. The map respects addition and multiplication, making equations at successive levels comparable.

Reduction is straightforward, but reversing it is a constrained lifting problem. A coarse solution can have several fine solutions above it or none satisfying the required equation. Choosing an arbitrary finer representative does not establish that it remains a solution.

glossary.definition: A sequence of solutions at successive levels whose reductions agree. A node at one finite level can have several children or no child.
explanation: A branch records consecutive choices of finer solutions above a common coarse starting point. Each new node must satisfy both its own equation and the reduction condition linking it to the previous node. This distinguishes a coherent path from unrelated solutions found at separate moduli.

Branching describes genuine ambiguity among possible next digits, while a dead end records a local obstruction to continuation. Reaching a fixed finite depth provides finite evidence. An infinite compatible solution requires an additional existence argument or an explicit compatible construction at all levels.

glossary.definition: A collection of objects with specified maps between levels and stated compatibility identities. For modular solutions, the next residue must reduce to the preceding one.
explanation: A tower includes the maps between its levels, so its meaning is more than a list of objects of increasing size. Compatibility ensures that moving between levels in the prescribed ways gives consistent results. Modular reduction is a concrete example of these connecting maps.

To pass to a limiting object, the tower must satisfy whatever hypotheses justify that passage in the chosen setting. Finite prefixes can demonstrate the intended structure and detect failures, but do not automatically supply a complete infinite branch, convergence or uniqueness theorem.

glossary.definition: For a prime p, an element of the inverse limit of the residue rings modulo pⁿ. It specifies a compatible residue at every positive level. A finite list of residues is only a truncation of that data.
explanation: A p-adic integer gives one consistent residue at every modulus pⁿ. These residues can be viewed as successive finite prefixes of an infinite base-p expansion. Agreement at more low-order digits means greater p-adic closeness, rather than closeness in the ordinary real absolute value.

A computer stores only a finite prefix or another finite description, so its output usually represents a congruence class or enclosure at a chosen precision. Extending that data to a specific infinite object requires more information. P-adic integers also include values that are not ordinary nonnegative integers.

glossary.definition: A branch reaches the chosen last level without losing compatibility or the required equations. Survival to that level alone says nothing about the next one.
glossary.example_text: The residue 9 solves x² ≡ 1 modulo 16. Its only candidate lifts modulo 32 are 9 and 25, and both squares equal 17 modulo 32. This branch reaches level four but has no child at level five.
explanation: Survival means that the branch has met every tested requirement through the declared final level. The depth and equations checked belong with the reported result, because extending the modulus can introduce new constraints.

An absence of dead ends in a finite search does not by itself prove indefinite continuation. Conversely, the failure of one branch need not eliminate its siblings. A useful record preserves the actual parent-child links and stopping depth so that later work can distinguish a local branch failure from a global impossibility claim.

glossary.definition: The smallest subfield of a field. In characteristic p it consists of the p scalar classes and is isomorphic to Fₚ. In characteristic zero it is isomorphic to the rational numbers.
glossary.quick_example: The field F₅ has five elements. Its nonzero element 2 has inverse 3.
explanation: Every field contains a canonical copy of the arithmetic generated by its multiplicative identity and the required inverses. Positive characteristic gives the finite prime field Fₚ; characteristic zero gives a copy of Q. Other field elements can then be regarded as extending this starting scalar system.

The prime field should not be confused with every finite field of the same characteristic. F₂₅ contains F₅ but has additional elements and extension degree two over it. That distinction affects Frobenius, trace and norm formulas.

glossary.definition: A field containing a specified smaller field. The extension degree is its vector-space dimension over that smaller field.
explanation: An extension treats elements of a larger field as vectors over the smaller field. Its degree counts how many smaller-field coordinates are needed when that dimension is finite. A basis lets multiplication by a larger-field element be represented as a matrix over the smaller field.

This viewpoint defines the field trace and norm through ordinary matrix trace and determinant. The smaller field must be stated: the same larger field can have different dimensions over different subfields. Extending scalars can also make a polynomial split or introduce roots unavailable in the original field.

glossary.definition: In a finite field of characteristic p, the map x ↦ xᵖ is an automorphism. Over F_q, the relative Frobenius is x ↦ x^q. The example uses q = p = 5.
glossary.example_text: In F₂₅ = F₅[α] with α² = 3, one has α⁵ = −α. Thus Frobenius sends 1+α to 1−α, and applying it twice returns 1+α.
glossary.quick_example: In characteristic p, (a+b)ᵖ = aᵖ+bᵖ. On Fₚ itself the Frobenius fixes every element.
explanation: In characteristic p, the binomial coefficients between the endpoints vanish modulo p, giving (a+b)ᵖ=aᵖ+bᵖ. This makes the power map compatible with field addition as well as multiplication. Finiteness ensures that the injective field map is also surjective.

Relative Frobenius fixes the chosen base field F_q and organizes the conjugates in a finite extension. Its iterates enter trace and norm formulas. The exponent q and the extension degree therefore belong to the construction; the map is not ordinary numerical exponentiation used as an approximation.

glossary.definition: For a finite field extension L/K, the trace of the K-linear map that multiplies L by an element a. In F₂₅/F₅ it is a+a⁵.
explanation: Multiplication by a fixed extension-field element is a linear operation over the base field. Taking that operation’s matrix trace produces a scalar in the base field, independently of the basis used to represent multiplication.

For finite fields, the same trace is a sum of Frobenius conjugates. It is additive and base-field linear, unlike the multiplicative field norm. Although it is computed using a matrix trace, its input is an extension-field element rather than an arbitrary matrix or a vector length.

glossary.definition: For a finite field extension L/K, the determinant of multiplication by an element a as a K-linear map. In F₂₅/F₅ it is a·a⁵. This norm is algebraic and is not a vector length.
glossary.example_text: For β = 1+α in F₂₅ = F₅[α] with α² = 3, the norm to F₅ is ββ⁵ = (1+α)(1−α) = 1−3 = 3 in F₅.
explanation: The determinant of multiplication measures an algebraic multiplicative effect of one extension-field element on the whole extension space. Changing its basis does not change that determinant. In a finite-field extension it equals the product of the relevant Frobenius conjugates.

This norm is multiplicative, but it is not a nonnegative length satisfying a triangle inequality. Its values lie in the base field and can have finite-field arithmetic. Confusing it with a vector-space norm would give incorrect geometric or error interpretations.

glossary.definition: A nonconstant polynomial over a field that cannot be factored into two polynomials of positive degree over that field. For degree two, irreducibility is equivalent to having no root in the field.
explanation: Irreducibility depends on the coefficient field. A polynomial can resist factorization over one field and split over a larger extension. Over a field, quotienting the polynomial ring by an irreducible polynomial produces a field, which is a standard way to construct finite extensions.

The no-root test is sufficient for irreducibility only in degrees two and three. In higher degrees a polynomial can factor into nonconstant pieces without having a linear factor. Low-degree checks should therefore not be used as unrestricted irreducibility criteria.

glossary.definition: A system with addition, subtraction and commutative multiplication satisfying the ring laws and having a multiplicative identity. A nonzero element need not have a multiplicative inverse.
glossary.quick_example: The integers form a commutative ring with identity, but 2 has no multiplicative inverse within the integers.
explanation: A ring retains addition and multiplication while allowing more varied division behavior than a field. It may contain nonzero nonunits or zero divisors. The glossary’s convention is commutative and includes an identity, so those assumptions should be checked when another work uses the same word differently.

Linear algebra over rings becomes module theory: generators need not form a basis, and familiar rank arguments can require extra hypotheses. An equation solved by dividing by a nonzero element over a field may fail over a ring unless that element is actually invertible.

glossary.definition: An abelian additive group with a scalar action by a ring satisfying the usual distributive, associative, and identity laws. For a module over Q[t], multiplication by t can be specified by a Q-linear operator.
glossary.quick_example: An abelian group is a module over Z, where multiplying by an integer means repeated addition and its inverse.
explanation: A module generalizes a vector space by permitting scalars from a ring. The distributive rules still allow linear combinations, but the absence of division can produce torsion and prevent a module from having a basis.

For a Q[t]-module, the variable t acts as a chosen Q-linear operator. Polynomial relations in t then express operator relations on vectors. This connects generator questions and minimal-polynomial behavior to algebraic presentations, while keeping the scalar ring part of the model.

glossary.definition: A description of a module by generators and relations. A finite matrix A: Rᵐ → Rⁿ presents the quotient Rⁿ/im A.
explanation: Generators describe possible formal coordinates, while relations identify combinations that represent zero. A presentation matrix maps relation coordinates into generator coordinates, and taking its cokernel imposes those relations on the free generator module.

Different presentation matrices can describe isomorphic modules, so presentation-dependent entries should be distinguished from module invariants. The matrix’s sizes, coefficient ring and direction are essential. Over a general ring, treating it as an ordinary real matrix can discard the arithmetic structure the presentation was meant to retain.

glossary.definition: For a linear map or module map A: U → V, the quotient V/im A. It records target classes modulo those already reached by A.
glossary.quick_example: The cokernel of multiplication by 2 on Z is Z/2Z, which records the two parity classes.
explanation: The cokernel records what remains of the target after identifying outputs that differ by something already reachable. A target has zero cokernel class exactly when it lies in the original image. This makes the cokernel a natural place to describe missing directions in a repair problem.

It differs from the kernel, which describes erased input directions. In finite vector spaces, its dimension is codomain dimension minus rank. Over modules, its structure can contain torsion and multiplicity information that a dimension count alone would miss.

glossary.definition: An operator N for which Nᵏ = 0 for some positive integer k. It can be nonzero. The smallest such k on a nonzero space is its nilpotency index.
glossary.quick_example: N = [[0,1],[0,0]] is nonzero, but N² = 0.
explanation: Nilpotence means that sufficiently many repeated applications erase every input, even if earlier applications do something nontrivial. A coordinate shift that eventually moves every entry beyond the retained finite range is a basic model. For N²=0, applying N twice always gives zero, but applying it once can have a large effect.

Finite geometric identities then become exact: if Nᵏ=0, the inverse of I−N is I+N+⋯+Nᵏ⁻¹. No convergence argument is required. All eigenvalues of a nilpotent matrix are zero, which also illustrates why zero spectral radius does not imply that the operator itself or its one-step norm is zero.

glossary.definition: The ideal of ring elements that act as zero on every element of a module. For Q[t]/(tᵏ), the annihilator is the ideal (tᵏ).
glossary.quick_example: In the Z-module Z/6Z, every multiple of 6 acts as zero, so its annihilator is the ideal (6).
explanation: The annihilator records scalar operations that kill the entire module. For a Q[t]-module, it therefore describes polynomial operator relations holding on every vector, not merely on one selected input.

For Q[t]/(tᵏ), multiplication by tᵏ vanishes while lower powers can remain nonzero. The annihilator retains that exponent, unlike the underlying one-point support set. One can also define annihilators of individual elements; that is a related construction with a potentially larger set of killing scalars.

glossary.definition: The prime ideals at which a module’s localization is nonzero. In the example Q[t]/(tᵏ), the support is the single prime ideal (t). The underlying support set does not determine k or the module.
glossary.example_text: Over R = Q[t], the modules R/(t) and R/(t²) both have support {(t)}. Their rational dimensions are one and two, so equal support does not identify the modules.
explanation: Support asks where the module remains present after localizing at prime ideals. It is a set of locations in the algebraic sense, not a list of the module’s generators or a numerical support interval.

Modules can share this set while differing substantially in their internal structure. The family Q[t]/(tᵏ) always lives at the same prime (t), yet its length and rational dimension grow with k. Support therefore identifies where information remains, while invariants such as multiplicity describe how much structure remains there.

glossary.definition: For a finite presentation Rᵐ → Rⁿ → M → 0 over a commutative ring, the ideal generated by the n by n minors of the presentation matrix. In the one-generator example with relation tᵏ, it is (tᵏ).
explanation: The zeroth Fitting ideal extracts a presentation-independent ideal from maximal minors of a finite presentation matrix. In the one-generator case it simply retains the relation element, making the tutorial’s ideal (tᵏ) directly visible.

Its ideal structure can distinguish modules whose support sets agree. Passing to only the set of primes containing that ideal can discard exponents and other information. The zeroth convention and finite-presentation assumptions matter, especially when there are too few columns to form the displayed minors.

glossary.definition: For Q[t]/(tᵏ) supported at t=0, the integer k records the module’s length and its Q-vector-space dimension. This is additional data beyond the one-point support set. Other works use multiplicity with their own specified objects.
glossary.example_text: The module Q[t]/(t²) has basis (1,t) over Q and multiplicity two in this example. Its fiber at t = 0 still has dimension one. That special-fiber dimension does not recover the full module’s rational dimension.
explanation: Multiplicity measures additional structure at an already identified location. In the tutorial, 1,t,…,tᵏ⁻¹ remain as independent rational classes in Q[t]/(tᵏ), so k counts the module’s rational dimension and its length at that support point.

Knowing that the support is {(t)} does not reveal this count. The example separates location from retained algebraic thickness. Other uses of multiplicity, such as root or eigenvalue multiplicity, require their own definitions rather than inheriting the module example’s interpretation automatically.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix A with A* = A. Its diagonal entries are real and opposite off-diagonal entries are complex conjugates. This condition alone does not imply positivity.
glossary.quick_example: The matrix [[1,i],[−i,2]] is Hermitian because conjugating and transposing returns it.
explanation: Hermitian matrices are the complex analogue of real symmetric matrices. In finite dimensions they have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, making their quadratic forms real-valued and supporting their use as observables.

Real eigenvalues can still be negative. Positivity is an additional condition checked by the signs of the quadratic form or eigenvalues. Thus an observable can be Hermitian without being a density matrix, and a trace-one Hermitian matrix need not represent a state.

glossary.definition: A Hermitian matrix A for which v*Av is nonnegative for every vector v. Zero eigenvalues are allowed.
glossary.quick_example: [[1,1],[1,1]] is positive semidefinite because its quadratic form is |x+y|², and it has a nonzero kernel.
explanation: Positive semidefiniteness rules out negative quadratic energy in every direction while allowing invisible zero directions. For finite Hermitian matrices it is equivalent to all eigenvalues being nonnegative. One exact negative quadratic-form value is enough to disprove it.

This condition appears in density matrices, covariance matrices, Gram operators and Pick feasibility matrices, but their other constraints differ. Singular cases also need care in block elimination: replacing an inverse by a pseudoinverse without a range condition can miss an actual positivity obstruction.

glossary.definition: Off-diagonal density-matrix entries that encode relations between different basis components. They can contribute to probabilities after a change of measurement basis.
explanation: Coherence records relationships between components, not additional classical populations. Off-diagonal entries contribute cross terms when a measurement mixes the chosen basis vectors. Their complex phases can therefore affect interference while leaving coordinate probabilities fixed.

The description is basis-dependent. A matrix diagonal in one basis can have off-diagonal entries in another. Dephasing specifies which basis or subspace family defines the discarded coherence, so saying that coherence was removed without naming that decomposition leaves the operation ambiguous.

glossary.definition: An additive subgroup of a commutative ring closed under multiplication by every element of the ring. The principal ideal (f) consists of all multiples of f.
glossary.quick_example: The even integers form the ideal (2) in Z: multiplying an even integer by any integer stays even.
explanation: An ideal contains scalar combinations that remain within it even after multiplication by arbitrary ring elements. This absorption property allows a quotient ring to have well-defined multiplication, because changing a representative by an ideal element does not change its product class.

A principal ideal (f) records all multiples of one element. Different generators can give the same ideal when they differ by a unit. Ideals are therefore more structural than the choice of one displayed equation, and they underlie annihilators, Fitting invariants and prime-local support.

glossary.definition: A proper ideal P such that ab in P implies a in P or b in P. The ideal (t) in Q[t] is prime because the quotient is the field Q.
explanation: Primality says that a product can vanish in the quotient only if one of its factors vanishes there. Equivalently, quotienting a commutative ring by a prime ideal gives an integral domain. Requiring the ideal to be proper excludes the whole ring.

A prime ideal need not always give a field quotient; that stronger condition corresponds to maximality. The example (t) in Q[t] has a field quotient and hence satisfies both. Prime ideals provide the locations used in localization and module support.

glossary.definition: A construction that makes ring elements outside a chosen prime ideal invertible, and carries a module along with that scalar change. The prime lies in the module’s support exactly when the localized module is nonzero.
explanation: Localization permits division by a specified collection of elements, here those outside a chosen prime ideal. It changes which scalar operations are invertible while retaining the algebraic information relevant near that prime.

Some module elements or whole modules can disappear after this scalar change. The support records exactly the primes where the localized module does not vanish. This is an algebraic construction; interpreting it as ordinary numerical zooming or limiting requires additional explanation rather than following from the name alone.

glossary.definition: A declared finite collection of claim nodes, admissible leaves, and recorded inference rules. Certificate validity is relative to this supplied system.
explanation: A proof field supplies the ambient vocabulary and certified rules within which a certificate is judged. Its claim nodes identify obligations, its admissible leaves specify allowed starting points, and its rules say which conclusions can follow from available premises.

Validity is relative to that supplied system. A checker can establish that a target is reached using the recorded rules without proving the soundness of arbitrary replacement rules or the adequacy of the field for every mathematical question. Changing the ambient field can change which certificates exist and what their optimal costs are.

glossary.definition: A node allowed as a starting point under the declared proof-field contract. Selecting such a leaf does not require deriving it again inside that certificate.
explanation: An admissible leaf is a permitted foundation for the current certificate, such as an accepted premise or an already certified result. It does not need a derivation inside that certificate because the proof-field contract has assigned it that starting role.

This is a scoped permission, not a declaration that any arbitrary claim is true. Its justification can reside in an external proof or evidence record. When a certificate is moved to another proof field or source edition, the leaf’s admissibility must be checked again against that new contract.

glossary.definition: A specified set of premise nodes together with a conclusion node. The certificate can use the rule only when the required premises have been derived and its recorded certification permits it.
explanation: A rule connects a specified collection of premises to a conclusion. A rule requiring {a,b,c,d} cannot fire merely because three premises are available. All required premises and the rule’s recorded certification must be present under the current checking contract.

Using a rule several times can share already established premises, depending on the system’s representation. This affects certificate cost and graph structure. A valid derivation uses permitted rules correctly; it does not establish that an unverified implication inserted into the rule list is mathematically sound.

glossary.definition: The nodes obtainable by admitting selected admissible leaves and repeatedly applying the retained certified rules whose premises are available.
explanation: Closure is obtained by repeatedly adding conclusions whose retained rules have all their premises available. In a finite supplied field, this process reaches a stage at which no new nodes can be added. A target in that closure is reachable from the selected starting evidence.

The result depends on both selected leaves and selected rules. Omitting a needed rule can make one proposed certificate fail even when another valid certificate exists in the ambient field. Closure checks validity for the proposal; searching for a least or cheapest valid proposal is a separate problem.

glossary.definition: A valid node-and-rule certificate with no valid strictly smaller subcertificate under componentwise inclusion. Several incomparable minimal certificates can exist.
glossary.example_text: The certificate built from leaves s₁ and s₃ derives a, b, c and d, then the target t. Removing either selected leaf or any of its five retained rules breaks that derivation, so this certificate is inclusion-minimal.
explanation: Inclusion-minimality asks whether any selected node or rule can be removed while retaining a valid smaller certificate. It is a local statement in the inclusion order: no strictly smaller valid subcertificate exists inside that selected certificate.

It does not say that another incomparable certificate uses fewer items or costs less. Several minimal certificates can reach the same target through different leaves and rules. To compare all valid certificates by cost, cardinality or a least-element property, one must solve the corresponding stronger and differently ordered problem.

glossary.definition: A certificate contained componentwise in every certificate for the same request and rule system. This is stronger than being inclusion-minimal or having minimum numerical cost.
glossary.example_text: The two optimal certificates start from {s₁,s₃} and {s₂,s₄}. Their intersection contains no admissible leaf. With no mandatory starting leaves, it cannot derive t, so there is no least certificate in this rule system.
explanation: A least certificate would be a common valid core contained in every valid certificate for the same request. This is stronger than being impossible to shrink: it compares the candidate with all alternatives, including incomparable ones.

In the shared-premise example, two different pairs of leaves each reach the target, but their common selected evidence cannot start a derivation. Consequently no certificate can lie validly inside both, and no least certificate exists. Minimum cost can still exist despite this failure of a least element.

glossary.definition: A valid certificate attaining the lowest declared total cost among the permitted certificates. Costs count selected items according to the supplied rule, so a shared premise need not be charged each time it is used.
glossary.example_text: Each selected leaf costs one and supplies two of four required obligations. Either pair {s₁,s₃} or {s₂,s₄} reaches the target at cost two, while zero or one leaf cannot. Reusing a selected leaf for two consequences does not double its cost.
explanation: Minimum cost compares valid certificates using a declared numerical objective. The objective may charge selected leaves once even when several later rules reuse them. Shared premises can therefore make the cheapest derivation different from one obtained by independently minimizing each branch.

Proving optimality requires both a valid certificate of the stated cost and a lower-bound argument excluding cheaper allowed certificates. The result belongs to the supplied field and cost model. It need not identify a unique certificate, a least certificate under inclusion or the shortest proof in every possible proof system.

glossary.definition: The state coordinates or summary retained for a specified prediction task. A visible value need not contain enough information to determine its own next value.
explanation: Visible state is the information retained by the chosen observation, not necessarily the complete physical or mathematical state. Two full states can have the same current visible value while containing different hidden data.

Whether that visible value is enough depends on the prediction task. It may determine the present observation exactly yet fail to determine the next one. Testing for autonomous visible dynamics therefore requires comparing future visible outputs of all admissible full states sharing the same current summary.

glossary.definition: The part of the declared full state omitted by the current observation or summary. It can influence later visible outputs even when it does not affect the current output.
explanation: Hidden state includes whatever the current representation omits. Its significance comes from how the full dynamics couples it to the visible coordinates, not from whether it is directly measured now. An initially invisible difference can return to the visible part later.

The block update makes those pathways explicit through visible-to-hidden, hidden-to-hidden and hidden-to-visible maps. Ignoring the hidden state can introduce memory into the visible equation. A preparation fixing hidden coordinates reduces one kind of ambiguity, but need not make every later visible state sufficient on its own.

glossary.definition: An initialization that fixes the hidden coordinates by a specified rule. The example uses R(y)=(y,0). Results for this preparation need not hold for arbitrary hidden starting values.
explanation: A preparation specifies which full state is associated with a retained initial value. The map R(y)=(y,0) chooses zero hidden coordinates, so predictions from that preparation do not need to consider arbitrary initial hidden values.

After evolution, the hidden coordinates may no longer satisfy the preparation rule. Restarting the same preparation from a later visible value can therefore reset information that uninterrupted evolution retained. This explains why prepared visible evolution maps can fail the semigroup law even when the full state evolves autonomously.

glossary.definition: For the block update (y,z) ↦ (Ay+Bz,Gy+Dz), the maps Mₖ=BDᵏG describe a visible-to-hidden entry, k hidden transitions, and a return. The first effect of Mₖ on prepared visible evolution occurs after k+2 full steps.
glossary.example_text: For A = B = G = 1 and D = 0 in the visible and hidden block update, M₀ = BD⁰G = 1 while Mₖ = 0 for k ≥ 1. Information entering the hidden coordinate returns after two full steps.
explanation: The product BDᵏG follows a specific information path: enter hidden coordinates through G, spend k additional transitions there through D, then return through B. Its contribution is delayed because entry and return each consume a full step.

Eliminating hidden variables from the visible equation produces such delayed contributions from past visible states. Vanishing later memory maps can simplify the recurrence without making the current visible value alone sufficient. The permitted hidden initialization and the complete block model must remain attached to any claimed memory-free reduction.

glossary.definition: A transition rule determined by the retained current state, under the declared controls and initialization contract. For deterministic maps, full states with the same summary must have the same next summary.
explanation: An autonomous retained description has enough present information to determine its own next state under the stated contract. It does not need to inspect an unrecorded hidden coordinate or reconstruct an unspecified past history at each update.

For a deterministic summary, the decisive test is whether equal present summaries always yield equal next summaries. In the unrestricted linear setting, this becomes invariance of the summary kernel under the full update. A rule valid only for chosen representatives or prepared states has a narrower scope.

glossary.definition: Enlarging a retained state with additional coordinates or history needed for future prediction. The hidden-memory example retains the previous visible value along with the current one.
explanation: Augmentation retains information that a smaller state discarded, such as an extra coordinate, a delayed sample or a sufficient history statistic. The aim is to make future prediction depend only on the augmented present value.

In the Fibonacci example, retaining the preceding visible value supplies the missing hidden contribution and gives a two-coordinate autonomous update. More storage alone does not guarantee sufficiency: the added data must actually distinguish full states whose future requested outputs differ. Minimal augmentation is a separate optimization question.

glossary.definition: The identity Eₘ₊ₙ=EₘEₙ for nonnegative step counts, with E₀ the identity. It expresses agreement between uninterrupted evolution and successive uses of the same state-level evolution maps.
glossary.example_text: With the hidden coordinate initialized to zero, the prepared visible maps Eₙ = CTⁿR are scalar multipliers with E₁ = 1 and E₂ = 2. Thus E₂ ≠ E₁E₁. Restarting from the visible value resets hidden information.
explanation: The law says that evolving for n steps and then m more steps agrees with evolving for m+n steps in one uninterrupted run. The maps must act on the same sufficient state description, with compatible controls and initialization conventions.

Prepared visible maps can violate this law because composing them silently reapplies the preparation and resets hidden state. Such a failure does not contradict the semigroup behavior of the full autonomous dynamics. It identifies information omitted by the retained description or changed by the restart contract.

glossary.definition: Supplied input-output pairs for an unknown operation. For a linear operation, every linear relation among calibrated inputs must be respected by the supplied outputs.
explanation: Calibration constrains an unknown operation by supplying its values on selected inputs. If the operation is assumed linear, a relation among those inputs must give the corresponding relation among outputs. Inconsistent assignments cannot be repaired merely by choosing another linear extension.

Consistent data determine the operation on the calibrated span, but generally leave its behavior outside that span open. A one-step prediction can consequently be determined while a later prediction becomes ambiguous after the trajectory leaves the known region. Structural assumptions can reduce that ambiguity and must be stated explicitly.

glossary.definition: The span of the calibrated input vectors. Consistent exact linear calibration determines the operation on this span. Its outputs can leave that span.
glossary.example_text: The measurements Te₁ = e₁ and Te₂ = e₃ determine T(ae₁+be₂) = ae₁+be₃ throughout U = span(e₁,e₂). In particular, T(2e₁−e₂) = 2e₁−e₃, while Te₃ remains unspecified.
explanation: Linearity extends calibrated values to all linear combinations of the calibrated inputs. This gives a complete known restriction on their span when the supplied input-output relations are consistent. It does not determine values on independent directions outside that span.

The known outputs can themselves leave the calibrated span. In that case, applying the operation again may require uncalibrated information. Identifying a subspace that stays inside the known region under all allowed operations is what supports reusable multi-step predictions in the tutorial.

glossary.definition: A model satisfying all supplied data and every declared structural assumption. In the calibration example, all linear extensions of the known restriction are allowed, and each model stays fixed through a trajectory.
explanation: A compatible model is one complete interpretation of the unknown operation that satisfies all supplied constraints. Comparing these models reveals which conclusions follow from the data and which depend on an extra choice.

In the calibration example, choosing a model fixes its linear extension throughout a trajectory. One cannot change that extension independently at each step and still claim to be analyzing one fixed model. Additional positivity, symmetry or physical assumptions would restrict the model class and can change identifiability conclusions.

glossary.definition: A linear map on a larger vector space that agrees with a given map on its original subspace. Values on an added basis can vary unless further conditions are imposed.
explanation: To extend a linear map, choose a basis of the known subspace and complete it to a basis of the larger space. Values on the added basis vectors specify the previously unconstrained part, while the original basis values retain the known restriction.

This construction explains why exact calibration can leave many compatible models. It establishes algebraic extensions under the stated vector-space setting, not necessarily extensions satisfying extra norm, positivity or circuit constraints. Those additional structures need their own existence and uniqueness analysis.

glossary.definition: For the tutorial’s unrestricted linear extension class and full-state output, the largest subspace inside the calibration span preserved by every calibrated operation. All finite operation sequences from this subspace are determined by the calibration.
glossary.example_text: With Te₁ = e₁ and Te₂ = e₃, the known image of ae₁+be₂ stays in U = span(e₁,e₂) exactly when b = 0. The retained domain stabilizes at span(e₁), where every compatible extension satisfies Tⁿ(ae₁) = ae₁ for all n ≥ 0.
explanation: The reusable core identifies starting vectors whose allowed operation sequences stay within the region controlled by calibration. One-step knowledge is insufficient if the resulting vector can leave that known region before the next operation is applied.

Within the tutorial’s unrestricted linear-extension and full-state-output contract, preserving a subspace inside the calibration span ensures that all finite continuations remain determined there. Changing the model class or asking only for a partial output can change the appropriate core, so this definition should not be generalized without restating the task.

glossary.term: Identifiability relative to a model class
glossary.definition: A requested quantity is identifiable from the supplied data when every compatible model gives the same value. Identifying a particular output can require less information than identifying the whole model.
glossary.quick_example: Observing only x+y cannot distinguish parameter pairs (1,2) and (2,1) if both are allowed.
explanation: Identifiability asks whether the available evidence forces one answer across all models still allowed by the assumptions. It is a uniqueness-of-consequence question, not necessarily uniqueness of the whole underlying model.

Several different models can agree on a requested prediction even when their unobserved parameters differ. Conversely, selecting one convenient fitted model does not establish that its prediction is identifiable. To disprove identifiability, exhibit compatible models with different requested values; to establish it, show that every compatible model agrees.

glossary.definition: For n≥1, differentiating a power-series term aₙzⁿ gives n aₙzⁿ⁻¹. Constant terms differentiate to zero. Formal differentiation acts on coefficients. An analytic interpretation uses the function’s convergence and differentiability conditions.
explanation: Formal differentiation changes the coefficient list according to the monomial rule, without asking where a function converges. It lowers degree and weights the contribution by the original exponent. In an exponential normalization, the factorials reorganize this operation into a simpler shift of stored sequence entries.

Transporting differentiation through a basis change can produce a different-looking target operator. The falling-factorial map sends the source derivative to forward difference, not to ordinary differentiation in the target variable. Analytic differentiation and infinite termwise operations additionally require their stated convergence setting.

glossary.definition: An equation relating an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives. The example also evaluates the same function at contracted arguments qz and rz.
explanation: A differential equation constrains an unknown function through its rates of change, rather than merely listing its values. A power-series approach substitutes an unknown coefficient sequence and compares like degrees, converting the equation into algebraic relationships among those coefficients.

The feedback example also uses values at scaled arguments, so the recurrence must include the corresponding powers of the contraction factors. Solving the formal coefficient equations does not alone establish an analytic solution or its convergence interval. Existence, uniqueness and evaluation error require the hypotheses of the particular equation.

glossary.definition: A specified value, or collection of derivative values, used with a differential equation. The feedback example fixes T(0)=0, and the equation then forces T′(0)=1.
explanation: Initial data select among functions that satisfy a differential equation. The number and type of conditions needed depend on the equation, its order and its domain. A value at zero can also enter the coefficient recurrence as its starting coefficient.

Some derivative values are consequences of the equation rather than independent choices. In the stated feedback example, imposing T(0)=0 makes the equation force T′(0)=1. Assigning an incompatible derivative value as extra data would therefore change the problem into an inconsistent one.

glossary.definition: Evaluation at qz with 0<q<1 in the feedback example. A term cₙzⁿ becomes cₙqⁿzⁿ after this substitution. The scaling is inside the defining equation.
explanation: Replacing z by qz scales each degree-n coefficient contribution by qⁿ. For 0<q<1, higher degrees receive progressively stronger scaling at the same argument. This operation changes the input to the function; it is different from multiplying the whole output by q.

When the scaled function appears inside an equation, these degree-dependent factors belong in its coefficient recurrence. Their presence can influence convergence or bounds, but the contraction factor by itself does not settle those questions for an arbitrary nonlinear feedback equation.

glossary.definition: A rule determining successive series coefficients from earlier ones. It gives exact finite calculations at each degree. Analytic convergence and bounds for a discarded tail require additional arguments.
explanation: A recurrence turns a series construction into successive finite tasks: compute a new coefficient from coefficients already determined. It makes the calculation reproducible and can expose indexing, sign or normalization errors through low-degree checks.

The recurrence may establish a unique formal solution without proving that its series converges at a chosen argument. To use a finite prefix for numerical evaluation, one still needs a bound for the remaining coefficients or another remainder argument. Exact prefix arithmetic and analytic tail control answer different questions.

glossary.definition: An allowed vector added to the span of the original image so that a required target can become reachable. Both the target equation and the permitted coefficient system must remain specified.
explanation: A repair direction adds a permitted way to move beyond the outputs already attainable. If a target is outside the original image, its class in the cokernel records the missing part. A useful added direction must address that missing class rather than merely duplicate an existing image direction.

The allowed coefficient system and admissibility rules matter. Rational linear combinations, nonnegative combinations and discrete component selections define different repair problems. A direction that repairs the unrestricted linear span may therefore fail to be an allowable physical or menu-constrained repair.

glossary.definition: A repair problem allowing freely chosen added directions over the declared field. In the rational finite-dimensional setting, the minimum added dimension is the dimension of the span of the target residual classes in the original cokernel.
explanation: Free linear repair asks how much new span is needed when added directions can be chosen without a finite menu restriction. Passing to the original cokernel removes directions already available. The span of the target residual classes then measures the independent missing directions in the stated finite-dimensional linear model.

This dimension count concerns added linear freedom, not necessarily the number or cost of physical components. Restricting candidates to a supplied menu can require more selected choices or make repair impossible. Claims about minimum repair should therefore retain whether the choices are free or constrained.

glossary.definition: A supplied finite list of candidate directions, with costs and any selection restrictions. Feasibility and optimality are judged using this list and the original target equation.
explanation: A repair menu turns a free existence question into a constrained selection problem. Each candidate has specified mathematical effects, and costs or compatibility rules determine which subsets may be used together. Solving the resulting problem requires both reachability of the target and compliance with those selection rules.

A cheap candidate may add no new direction, while a more expensive candidate may resolve several target residuals at once. Counting only the dimension of the missing span can therefore miss the actual menu optimum. Exhaustive search establishes an optimum only over the declared finite candidate population and cost model.

glossary.definition: The declared cost of the selected repair choices. In the tutorial it is the sum of their selection costs, paid once per choice, independently of the rational coefficients used to combine them.
explanation: A cost model says what is charged: selected directions, repeated uses, coefficient magnitudes, hardware resources or something else. In the tutorial, paying once for a selected candidate differs from charging each algebraic use or each nonzero coefficient.

Optimality is meaningful only after this convention is fixed. Changing a candidate’s price or allowing a new repair can change the cheapest solution while leaving feasibility unchanged. A minimum-cost repair need not be unique, and it need not be the smallest repair under a different inclusion or dimension ordering.

glossary.definition: Existence of a solution satisfying the stated equations and admissibility conditions. Failure of one candidate or exhaustion of a search budget does not by itself show infeasibility.
explanation: Feasibility asks whether at least one allowed solution exists, before asking which is best. The allowed set includes the equations, input restrictions, coefficient field and any positivity or topology constraints. Removing or weakening a restriction changes the problem whose feasibility is being assessed.

A valid witness proves feasibility by satisfying those requirements. Infeasibility needs a reason excluding every allowed witness, such as a separating linear functional or an exhaustive argument over a finite domain. A rejected candidate or timed-out solver leaves a more limited conclusion.

glossary.definition: A linear functional that annihilates every allowed direction but has a nonzero value on the required target. It proves that this target lies outside their span under the stated linear problem.
explanation: The witness turns an impossible vector equation into an impossible scalar equation. If ℓ annihilates every allowed direction, it also annihilates every linear combination of them. A target with ℓ(t)≠0 therefore cannot lie in that span.

This is a checkable certificate for the specified unrestricted linear problem. Its hypotheses must still match the allowed directions and field. More restrictive problems, such as nonnegative combinations or fixed circuit topologies, can have additional obstructions that are not captured merely by exclusion from a linear span.

glossary.definition: A model with a Gaussian state and specified linear observations with Gaussian noise. The tutorial supplies an independent noise variable, a prior mean and covariance, an observation matrix and a positive noise variance.
explanation: The model specifies a prior state distribution and an observation mechanism, including the noise distribution and its independence assumptions. Linearity and Gaussian structure make the conditional mean and covariance computable through explicit finite matrix formulas.

Those formulas are exact consequences of the declared probabilistic model, not universal guarantees that the model matches observed reality. Changing noise dependence, covariance assumptions or observation nonlinearity can change the posterior calculation. Exact rational matrix arithmetic can verify an example’s algebra without validating its statistical assumptions.

glossary.definition: The state distribution specified before conditioning on the observation under the declared model. A Gaussian prior is described by its mean and covariance.
explanation: The prior records the distribution used before incorporating the particular observation under discussion. It can encode earlier evidence or modeling assumptions; the word does not mean that it must precede every observation in the entire history of a problem.

Its mean and covariance influence how strongly a Gaussian update responds to new data. Two different priors can produce different posteriors from the same likelihood. Once the posterior is reused as a later prior, the new observation and independence contract must be stated consistently.

glossary.definition: For a fixed observed value, the observation density viewed as a function of the proposed state or parameter. It is combined with the prior and normalized to obtain a posterior density when that density formula applies.
explanation: The likelihood holds the observed data fixed and varies the candidate state or parameter. It expresses how compatible those data are with different candidates under the observation model. As a function of the candidate, it need not integrate to one.

Bayesian updating multiplies this function by the prior and normalizes over the candidate state when the density formula applies. Confusing likelihood with the posterior omits that prior information and normalization. The chosen observation density and reference measure also belong to the model.

glossary.definition: The state distribution conditional on the observed data under the supplied prior and observation model. The tutorial computes the usual explicit Gaussian conditional density by completing the square.
explanation: The posterior incorporates the observed data through the specified prior and observation law. In the tutorial’s linear Gaussian setting, completing the quadratic exponent gives another Gaussian distribution with an updated mean and covariance.

It describes conditional uncertainty under that model, rather than certainty about the true state or proof of model adequacy. A narrow posterior can still be misleading if the observation or noise assumptions are wrong. Singular Gaussian models require care because an ordinary full-dimensional density or inverse covariance may be unavailable.

glossary.definition: For a random vector X with mean m and finite second moments, the matrix E[(X−m)(X−m)ᵀ]. Its diagonal entries are variances. For a unit direction u, uᵀCu is the variance in that direction.
glossary.quick_example: Independent coordinates with variances 1 and 4 have covariance matrix diag(1,4).
explanation: Covariance measures fluctuations around the mean and their pairwise relationships. Its diagonal gives individual variances, while off-diagonal entries describe how coordinates vary together. Every real covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every scalar projection has nonnegative variance.

The matrix changes with the coordinate system and its units. Zero covariance implies independence for jointly Gaussian coordinates, but not for arbitrary distributions. Singular covariance means that some linear direction has zero variance, so an ordinary precision-matrix inverse is unavailable there.

glossary.definition: The inverse covariance when the covariance is invertible. In a nonsingular Gaussian density it appears in the quadratic exponent. This use of precision is distinct from the number of bits in stored arithmetic.
glossary.quick_example: For covariance diag(1,4), the precision matrix is diag(1,1/4).
explanation: The precision matrix weights deviations in the exponent of a nonsingular Gaussian density. Directions with smaller covariance receive stronger quadratic penalties after inversion. Off-diagonal precision structure has its own interpretation and should not be read as simply the reciprocal of each covariance entry.

The inverse exists only when covariance is nonsingular. A singular Gaussian distribution can still be valid, but needs a suitable lower-dimensional or generalized formulation. Arithmetic precision, measured in stored bits, is an unrelated use of the same word.

glossary.definition: The difference d=y−Hm between an observation and its predicted mean in the linear model. Its covariance is S=HPHᵀ+R when the state covariance is P and the independent noise covariance is R.
glossary.quick_example: If an observation is 7 and the predicted observation is 5, the innovation is 2 under the observation-minus-prediction convention.
explanation: The innovation measures how surprising the observation is relative to its predicted mean before updating. Its covariance includes both projected state uncertainty and observation noise, so a given discrepancy can have different significance at different uncertainty scales.
