glossary.definition: A nonnegative square root of an eigenvalue of A*A for a real or complex matrix A, with zero-padding conventions stated when needed. The largest singular value is the induced Euclidean operator norm. Singular values describe gain and rank without requiring A to be square.
glossary.quick_example: For A = [[0,2],[3,0]], A*A = diag(9,4), so its singular values are 3 and 2.
glossary.note: A small computed singular value needs a tolerance or enclosure before it is treated as exactly zero.
explanation: Singular values describe how strongly a matrix stretches orthogonal input directions after suitable unitary coordinate choices. A zero singular value corresponds to an erased direction; positive ones describe retained gains. This viewpoint applies to rectangular maps, including analysis maps with more measurements than input coordinates.

They differ from eigenvalues because the input and output directions need not be the same. A nonzero nilpotent matrix has only zero eigenvalues but still has positive gain on some inputs. Very small singular values identify sensitive recovery directions, although deciding that one is exactly zero requires more than a floating-point threshold.

glossary.definition: A factorization A = UΣV* of a finite real or complex matrix, where U and V are orthogonal or unitary and Σ is rectangular diagonal with nonnegative entries. These entries are the singular values. It separates input directions, gains and output directions.
glossary.quick_example: The diagonal matrix diag(3,1) already has an SVD with U = V = I and Σ = diag(3,1).
glossary.note: Truncating an SVD changes the operator unless all omitted singular values are zero.
explanation: Read the factorization from right to left: V* changes to orthonormal input coordinates, Σ scales or erases those coordinates, and U places the results in orthonormal output coordinates. This separates geometry from gain and reveals the map’s rank through its positive singular values.

The same factorization constructs the Moore–Penrose inverse by reciprocating positive singular values and leaving zero ones at zero. Truncating small positive values is an approximation choice, not exact inversion. Such truncation can improve numerical robustness, but its threshold and resulting residual must be reported with the calculation.

glossary.definition: A complex square matrix T satisfying T*T = TT*. In finite complex dimensions, normal matrices admit an orthonormal eigenbasis. Hermitian and unitary matrices are normal; an arbitrary diagonalizable matrix need not be normal.
glossary.quick_example: The nonzero nilpotent matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] is not normal: T*T = diag(0,1), while TT* = diag(1,0).
explanation: Normality is the compatibility condition between an operator and its adjoint that permits a unitary eigenbasis over the complex numbers. In those coordinates, the operation consists of independent scalar actions without an oblique basis change. This makes spectral and Euclidean norm information fit together particularly well.

Hermitian and unitary matrices satisfy this condition for different reasons: one equals its adjoint, while the other has its adjoint as its inverse. A diagonalizable matrix with a poorly conditioned eigenbasis need not be normal. The property depends on the inner product through the adjoint, so it is not preserved by every arbitrary similarity change.

glossary.definition: For a finite real or complex matrix A, the norm defined by ‖A‖HS² = tr(A*A), equal to the sum of the squared absolute values of its entries. It measures matrix size in the specified orthonormal coordinates and differs from the largest-singular-value operator norm.
glossary.quick_example: For diag(3,4), the Hilbert–Schmidt norm is 5, while the induced Euclidean norm is 4.
explanation: This norm treats the matrix entries as one Euclidean vector of coefficients. Equivalently, it sums the squared gains over an orthonormal input basis, which makes it useful for total matrix discrepancy or density-matrix coherence calculations.

It differs from the induced Euclidean norm, which asks only for the largest gain in one direction. For a rank-r matrix, the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm is the sum of the r positive squared singular values. The finite matrix convention here should not be transferred unchanged to every infinite-dimensional operator.

glossary.definition: An operation U whose square is the identity: U² = I. Applying it twice restores the input. A linear involution over a field where 2 is invertible splits the space into its +1 and −1 eigenspaces via (I+U)/2 and (I−U)/2.
glossary.quick_example: Reflection of a polynomial, Uf(x) = f(−x), is an involution. Its +1 and −1 parts are the even and odd polynomials.
glossary.note: The identity U² = I does not by itself make U orthogonal or unitary.
explanation: An involution is a reversible operation whose inverse is itself. The first application may change an object, but the second restores it exactly. When 2 is invertible, averaging x with Ux selects the fixed part, while taking half their difference selects the sign-reversing part.

This explains the even–odd polynomial split under reflection f(x)↦f(−x). It also distinguishes involutions from projectors: a projector satisfies P²=P, whereas an involution satisfies U²=I. An involution can be oblique with respect to a chosen metric, so self-inversion alone does not guarantee length preservation.

glossary.definition: The set of outputs obtained from one input by the declared allowed operations. For a single operator T, its forward orbit is {v,Tv,T²v,…}. Taking the linear span of an orbit is a further step in the definition of a cyclic vector.
glossary.quick_example: If T swaps two coordinates, the orbit of (1,0) is {(1,0),(0,1)}; its span is all of R².
explanation: An orbit follows what the permitted action can actually reach from a starting object. With one forward operator, it records successive iterates. With a group action, inverses may also be allowed; with a typed system, only paths whose operations match the current type can be followed.

The orbit and its linear span answer different questions. A two-point orbit can span a two-dimensional space, and a finite cyclic orbit can impose a strict phase restriction even when every point has the same norm. Reachability arguments must specify the permitted action rather than replace it with all imaginable linear combinations or continuous motions.

glossary.definition: A retained description of an operation. For a projector P and operator T, PTP acts on the retained range. For a summary R and a chosen lift S, RTS is a candidate reduced operation. Exact agreement with all original inputs requires an additional compatibility condition.
glossary.quick_example: For T = [[1,2],[3,4]] and P = diag(1,0), PTP retains only the upper-left entry 1.
glossary.note: A compression can be useful even when the retained state does not determine its own exact future.
explanation: Compression replaces a full operation by one acting through a retained description. It can reduce storage or calculation, but its interpretation depends on the chosen summary and lift. Selecting a representative input is a modeling choice unless all inputs with the same summary give the same required output.

For PTP, inputs and outputs are restricted to the retained range. The omitted blocks describe what was lost. A useful approximation can tolerate a controlled residual; exact reduced dynamics instead require a compatibility or invariance argument that eliminates the relevant ambiguity for every admissible input.

glossary.definition: A linear map preserving the specified norm of every input. Between finite inner-product spaces, preserving inner products is equivalent. In orthonormal coordinates an isometric embedding Q satisfies Q*Q = I; it need not be onto its codomain.
glossary.quick_example: The map x ↦ (x,0) preserves Euclidean length. Its matrix is rectangular, so it is not a unitary automorphism of R².
explanation: An isometry retains the geometry measured by its stated norm. In inner-product coordinates, Q*Q=I says that its columns form an orthonormal family, so inner products of all input pairs are preserved. The map can embed a smaller space into a larger one without losing information.

The reverse product QQ* is then a projector onto the embedded image, not generally the identity on the whole codomain. This is the rectangular counterpart of an orthogonal or unitary coordinate change. Preserving one chosen norm also does not imply preserving every differently weighted coordinate norm.

glossary.definition: A scalar-valued function B(u,v) linear separately in u and v. Over the real numbers a matrix M gives B(u,v) = uᵀMv. Symmetry, positivity and nondegeneracy are additional properties rather than part of bilinearity.
glossary.quick_example: B(u,v) = u₁v₁−u₂v₂ is symmetric and bilinear, but B((0,1),(0,1)) = −1, so it is not an inner product.
glossary.note: For complex inner products one argument is conjugate-linear. That pairing is sesquilinear.
explanation: Bilinearity means that fixing either argument leaves a linear scalar question in the other. A matrix encodes those pairings between basis vectors, so the form can describe interactions or energies without being a positive notion of length. Symmetry and positivity should therefore be checked explicitly.

When coordinates change by y=Cx, a real bilinear-form matrix transforms by inverse factors on both sides, rather than by operator conjugation. For a quadratic expression xᵀMx, the corresponding matrix is C⁻ᵀMC⁻¹. This difference reflects the fact that the form consumes two vector arguments and returns a scalar.

glossary.definition: In the real finite-dimensional setting, a scalar expression q(x) = xᵀMx, usually written with M symmetric. In complex Hermitian geometry the corresponding real-valued expression is x*Mx with M Hermitian. Positivity asks whether this value is nonnegative for every input.
glossary.quick_example: With M = [[1,1],[1,1]], q(x,y) = (x+y)². It is nonnegative and vanishes on the nonzero direction (1,−1).
explanation: A quadratic form combines coordinates in pairs, including cross terms that record interaction between directions. With a symmetric real matrix, an off-diagonal entry appears twice in the expanded expression. For instance, the all-ones two-by-two matrix gives x²+2xy+y² rather than x²+xy+y².

Testing the sign on all vectors distinguishes positive definite, positive semidefinite and indefinite forms. A single negative value disproves positive semidefiniteness and can serve as an exact feasibility witness. In probability, evaluating such a form on a random vector gives a random variable; its distribution needs the vector’s law as additional data.

glossary.definition: A family of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is the whole set. Each element lies in exactly one block. A finer partition divides coarse blocks into smaller blocks; this set-theoretic use of block is distinct from an operator matrix block.
glossary.quick_example: The partition {{0,2},{1,3}} groups four indices by parity. The singleton partition refines it.
explanation: A partition specifies which elements are grouped together without overlaps or omissions. It can represent coarse observations, packet addresses or events whose internal distinctions are being ignored. A refinement splits existing blocks but does not mix elements from different coarse blocks.

In finite averaging, values are replaced by one weighted mean per block. The partition determines which observations remain visible, while the weights determine the averaging geometry. A partition of a set should not be confused with a decomposition of an operator into matrix blocks, although the two can be related by coordinate selectors.

glossary.term: Sufficient summary for a requested output
glossary.definition: A map R that retains enough information to determine a specified output F: there is a map G on the attained summary values such that F = G∘R. Equivalently, F is constant on each fiber of R. Sufficiency is relative to the requested output and admissible inputs.
glossary.quick_example: R(x,y) = x+y is sufficient for F(x,y) = 2(x+y), but is insufficient for recovering x on all of R².
glossary.note: This deterministic recovery definition is separate from statistical sufficiency for a family of probability laws.
explanation: Sufficiency is always relative to a question. Two inputs may differ in many ways but still be interchangeable if the requested output takes the same value on both. A summary is sufficient when it never merges inputs whose requested answers differ.

This viewpoint supports deliberate compression: retain exactly the distinctions needed by the task rather than require full input reconstruction. For a family of requested outputs, every member of that family must be constant on summary fibers. A summary sufficient for one present observation may still be insufficient for predicting future observations under an operation.

glossary.definition: For a vector space V and subspace K, the canonical linear map V → V/K sending x to its equivalence class x+K. Its kernel is K and it is surjective. It retains exactly the distinction between inputs differing by an element of K.
glossary.quick_example: Quotienting R² by span{(1,−1)} identifies all pairs with the same sum.
explanation: The quotient map formalizes forgetting an entire subspace of directions at once. It sends every x+k with k∈K to the same class as x. Its output is therefore an equivalence class, not a chosen representative or a numerical average.

Any linear map that annihilates K descends to a well-defined linear map on the quotient. This is the algebraic reason kernel inclusion appears in recovery. Choosing coordinates or representatives for the quotient is an additional construction, and choosing representatives alone does not restore the discarded distinctions.

glossary.definition: The size of an approximation error measured in a stated norm, such as |x−x̂| for scalars or ‖x−x̂‖ for vectors. It retains the units and scale of the quantity. An acceptance threshold must use the same units and norm.
glossary.quick_example: Approximating 100 by 99 gives absolute error 1, while approximating 0.001 by 0 gives absolute error 0.001.
explanation: Absolute error answers how large the discrepancy is in the quantity’s own units. An error of one volt, one coordinate unit or a stated vector norm can be interpreted without dividing by the target’s magnitude. This also makes the measure meaningful at a zero target.

Whether it is acceptably small still depends on the application’s scale. The same absolute discrepancy can be negligible for a large quantity and dominant for a small one. Report the norm and units before comparing absolute errors from different calculations or using them with a tolerance.

glossary.definition: An absolute error divided by a specified nonzero reference size. With exact target x, a common rule is ‖x−x̂‖/‖x‖ when x ≠ 0. The reference and zero-target rule must be stated.
glossary.quick_example: Approximating 100 by 99 gives relative error 1/100. Approximating 0.001 by 0 gives relative error 1.
glossary.note: A small absolute error can have a large relative error near zero.
explanation: Relative error compares the discrepancy with a declared reference size, producing a scale-free ratio when the units agree. It is useful when outputs span very different magnitudes and a fixed absolute threshold would treat them unevenly.

The denominator matters. Dividing by the exact target, the computed answer or an input scale produces different tests. At or near a zero target, a relative measure can be undefined or misleadingly large, so numerical contracts often combine a relative rule with a separately stated absolute rule.

glossary.definition: The difference between a computed output and the exact output of the declared problem on the declared input. A forward bound controls the answer directly. It can include effects from input uncertainty, operator approximation and finite arithmetic.
glossary.quick_example: For the equation 2x = 6, a computed answer x̂ = 2.9 has absolute forward error 0.1.
explanation: Forward error concerns the answer the user wanted: how far the computed output lies from the exact output for the same declared input. It is the most direct accuracy question, but the exact reference answer is often unavailable, so a bound must be derived indirectly.

An equation residual can support such a bound only when the problem’s stability is controlled. For a nonsingular linear system, applying A⁻¹ to the residual relates it to the solution error. The inverse’s norm explains why a small residual can coexist with a large forward error in an ill-conditioned problem.

glossary.definition: The size of an allowed perturbation to the input data that makes the computed answer an exact solution. The data components allowed to change and their norm determine the backward-error problem. Small backward error gives a useful forward guarantee only with suitable conditioning.
glossary.quick_example: For 2x = 6, x̂ = 2.9 exactly solves 2x = 5.8. If only the right side may change, that perturbation has absolute size 0.2.
explanation: Backward error changes the question from the output to the input data. It asks whether the computed answer is exactly right for a nearby permitted problem. The word permitted is essential: changing only a right-hand side differs from changing both a matrix and a right-hand side.

A backward-stable algorithm can return answers corresponding to small data perturbations, yet an ill-conditioned problem can still have large forward error. Separating algorithmic stability from problem conditioning helps identify whether the remedy is better arithmetic, a different algorithm or a better-posed model.

glossary.definition: Arithmetic on sets represented by intervals, with operations producing intervals that contain all allowed exact outputs. Finite implementations need outward rounding. Repeated occurrences of an uncertain quantity can widen an enclosure because interval endpoints do not record all dependencies.
glossary.quick_example: For x in [1,2], direct interval subtraction gives x−x in [−1,1], although the expression is identically zero when both occurrences denote the same x.
explanation: Intervals represent sets of possible exact values. Each operation returns a set guaranteed to include all corresponding outputs, provided the implementation encloses rounding as well. This supports validated bounds rather than a single estimate with an unexplained number of digits.

The enclosure can be conservative because ordinary intervals do not remember dependencies between repeated occurrences of a variable. Dividing by an interval containing zero also requires special treatment. A narrow final interval is useful only when all necessary input uncertainty and analytic approximation terms have been included.

glossary.definition: A linear map T between normed spaces for which a finite constant C satisfies ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖ for every input. Its induced norm is the least such bound. All linear maps between finite-dimensional normed spaces are bounded; infinite-dimensional cases need this hypothesis.
glossary.quick_example: Multiplication of every coordinate by 2 on Euclidean space is bounded with induced norm 2.
explanation: Boundedness is the existence of one finite amplification constant that works for every input. For linear maps on normed spaces it is equivalent to continuity, connecting an algebraic operation with control of limiting processes and small perturbations.

Finite-dimensional matrices have this property for the usual norms, but familiar infinite-dimensional operations can depend strongly on their chosen domain and norm. Differentiation, for example, cannot be assumed bounded merely because it is linear. The operator’s function space and norm must accompany an analytic stability argument.

glossary.definition: A recorded sequence of inference steps showing how admitted leaves and previously established conclusions reach a target. Each step must cite an allowed rule with all its premises available. Checking a trace establishes its validity within the declared rule system.
glossary.quick_example: Admit s₁ and s₃, derive a,b,c,d using their recorded rules, then apply {a,b,c,d} ⇒ t.
glossary.note: A valid trace in a supplied proof field does not establish the soundness of arbitrary externally supplied rules.
explanation: A trace exposes the order in which evidence becomes available. At each step, the checker verifies that the cited rule is permitted and that its premises have already been established or admitted. This makes the difference between a reachable target and a merely listed target inspectable.

The trace’s final validity depends on the ambient rule and leaf contract. A correct trace checker and a correct search implementation are separate obligations: the first can reject a bad proposal without proving that the search procedure will find every valid one or identify the cheapest one.

glossary.definition: An established node used by more than one later inference. Sharing allows a derivation to be represented as a directed acyclic graph instead of copying the whole premise derivation into each branch. Costs depend on whether reused nodes are charged once or once per use.
glossary.quick_example: In the certificate example, s₁ supplies both a and b but its selected-leaf cost is charged only once.
explanation: Sharing records one established fact as support for several later conclusions. It avoids copying the entire supporting derivation into each branch. A graph representation can therefore use fewer selected proof objects than a tree representation that duplicates every use.

The cost convention must say whether that shared object is charged once, once per use or in another way. In the tutorial, one selected leaf can discharge two obligations for one unit of cost. Optimizing branches separately can miss this benefit and overestimate the minimum cost of the whole certificate.

glossary.definition: An admissible instance on which a claimed universal conclusion fails. A counterexample must satisfy the claim’s hypotheses. For a recovery claim, two admissible inputs with the same summary and different requested outputs provide a collision counterexample.
glossary.quick_example: The pairs (1,0) and (0,1) have the same sum and different first coordinates, disproving recovery of the first coordinate from the sum alone.
explanation: A counterexample refutes the precise universal statement it satisfies the hypotheses of. Its strength is logical, not statistical: one genuine violating instance is enough to disprove a claim about every admissible input.

It should identify both the satisfied assumptions and the failed conclusion. A numerical discrepancy near a tolerance boundary may require exact arithmetic or an enclosure before it becomes a rigorous witness. Failure of a stronger statement also does not refute a weaker or more restricted statement that was actually claimed.

glossary.definition: A condition that must hold whenever a requested property holds. If A implies B, then B is necessary for A. Failing B rules out A, but passing B alone need not establish A.
glossary.quick_example: Equal reflection magnitude is necessary for cyclic reachability on the Smith chart. A prescribed finite rotation order also restricts the phase.
explanation: A necessary condition supplies a test every solution must pass. It is especially useful for ruling out candidates: violating the condition immediately excludes them from the requested class. Passing the test, however, may leave other independent requirements unresolved.

On a Smith-chart cyclic orbit, equal reflection magnitude is necessary because rotations preserve radius. A fixed finite rotation order also restricts phase, so matching radius alone is insufficient. This illustrates why a list of necessary conditions should not be described as a complete feasibility criterion without proving the converse.

glossary.definition: A condition that guarantees the requested property. If A implies B, then A is sufficient for B. The same implication makes B necessary for A. An equivalence provides both directions.
glossary.quick_example: For linear F and R on a common vector space, ker R contained in ker F is sufficient for recovering F from R on the whole space.
explanation: A sufficient condition gives a route to establishing the desired property. Once its hypotheses are verified, the implication guarantees the conclusion. It can be stronger than necessary, meaning that other valid cases may exist outside its scope.

For example, an invertible coordinate change is sufficient to transfer an operator by conjugation, but some noninvertible intertwiners also connect compatible operations. An equivalence or an if-and-only-if theorem proves both necessity and sufficiency; a one-direction argument establishes only the direction it actually proves.

glossary.definition: A search that has established neither a valid witness nor a proof that none exists within the specified problem. A timeout, an exhausted budget or rejection of one proposed certificate can leave the existence question unresolved.
glossary.quick_example: Rejecting the one-leaf proposal {s₁} leaves the valid two-leaf certificate {s₁,s₃} available.
explanation: An inconclusive search leaves the existence question unresolved. The procedure may have explored only part of the candidate space, exhausted a resource budget or failed to validate the candidate it happened to find. None of those outcomes by itself excludes valid candidates elsewhere.

A useful record distinguishes this status from infeasibility and from a checked witness. It should preserve the search bounds, stopping reason and any valid intermediate evidence. Later work can then continue from a known limitation instead of treating a timeout or a rejected proposal as an impossibility theorem.

glossary.definition: A proposition expressed in a proof assistant’s language with explicit types, hypotheses and conclusion. Its relationship to a written theorem depends on the interpretation of every object and assumption. A declaration name alone does not specify that relationship.
glossary.quick_example: A declaration proving a finite matrix identity covers that identity under its encoded hypotheses; it does not automatically cover an infinite-dimensional analogue.
explanation: A formal statement makes types, assumptions and quantifiers part of an expression that a proof assistant can check. Small differences in those details can change its meaning substantially, even when its declaration name resembles a familiar written theorem.

To establish correspondence, compare the full formal type with the written claim and explain how its objects are interpreted. An encoded finite model can prove useful selected facts without covering an unrestricted infinite-dimensional claim. Successful compilation confirms the accepted formal development, not every informal interpretation attached to it.

glossary.definition: A computation with enough recorded inputs, source identity, environment information and instructions to repeat the stated check. Reproduction should compare the promised outputs or invariants. Repeating a calculation preserves the scope of the calculation rather than extending it.
glossary.quick_example: A source archive, its hash, the arithmetic convention and the expected rational output let another reader replay one exact example.
explanation: Reproducibility makes a claimed run repeatable on identified inputs with identified code and conventions. Source hashes, commands, versions and expected invariants help another reader distinguish a genuine replay from a similar calculation performed on changed data.

A reproduced result retains its original scope. Repeating finite tests does not establish untested asymptotic behavior, and reproducing an implementation’s output does not independently establish the implementation’s correctness. The strongest records keep execution success, mathematical interpretation and source-to-claim correspondence separate.

glossary.definition: For a nonzero polynomial, the largest exponent having a nonzero coefficient. Over a field, degrees add under multiplication of nonzero polynomials. The zero polynomial needs a separate convention, often degree −∞, when degree formulas include it.
glossary.quick_example: The polynomial 4−2x+3x³ has degree 3. A falling-factorial basis element b₃ also has ordinary degree 3.
explanation: Degree records the highest occupied ordinary-power position after zero coefficients are removed. It controls how finite polynomial operations change the size of a coefficient description: differentiation lowers it in characteristic zero, multiplication adds degrees for nonzero factors over a field, and translation does not raise it.

It is not the same as every packet address or eigenvalue label. A polynomial expressed in falling-factorial coordinates can mix ordinary-power residues after expansion. Positive characteristic can also make a derivative lose its expected leading term, so familiar degree arguments need their field assumptions.

glossary.definition: A nonzero polynomial whose highest-degree coefficient is one. A sequence with one monic polynomial of each degree gives an invertible triangular change from ordinary powers on every finite degree range.
glossary.quick_example: x(x−1)(x−2) = x³−3x²+2x is monic. The constant polynomial 1 is monic of degree zero.
explanation: Monicity fixes the leading scale of a polynomial while leaving its lower coefficients free. A degree-k monic polynomial differs from xᵏ only by lower-degree terms, which explains the triangular relationship with ordinary powers.

Having one such polynomial at each degree gives unique finite polynomial coordinates. The falling factorials use this fact even in coefficient rings where factorial division is unavailable. Monicity supplies an algebraic basis-change argument; it does not imply orthogonality, numerical conditioning or a particular multiplication rule in the new coordinates.

glossary.definition: A square matrix with every entry on one side of its diagonal zero. A unitriangular matrix also has all diagonal entries equal to one, so it is invertible over any field. Triangular coordinate maps let successive coefficients be recovered in order.
glossary.quick_example: The lower-triangular matrix [[1,0],[3,1]] sends (a,b) to (a,3a+b); recover b by subtracting 3a.
explanation: A triangular matrix organizes dependencies in one direction. In a lower-triangular system, the first equation determines the first unknown, then each following equation can use the earlier answers. Nonzero diagonal entries make this successive recovery possible over a field.

Triangular changes of polynomial basis arise because a degree-k basis polynomial uses only powers of degree at most k. Monic basis polynomials give diagonal entries one, so every finite degree truncation is invertible. An infinite triangular array still needs its intended coefficientwise or analytic interpretation stated separately.

glossary.definition: The least positive integer p for which adding the multiplicative identity to itself p times gives zero, if such an integer exists; otherwise the characteristic is zero. Positive field characteristic is always prime. Division by integers in formulas must respect this value.
glossary.quick_example: In the field with three elements, 1+1+1 = 0. A formula dividing by 3 cannot be used there.
glossary.note: Falling-factorial coordinate maps remain monic triangular in positive characteristic, but derivative and roots-of-unity arguments can require additional hypotheses.
explanation: Characteristic describes how ordinary integer coefficients are interpreted inside a field. In characteristic p, the integer p becomes zero, so factorials and denominators containing p cannot be inverted there. In characteristic zero, no positive integer becomes zero.

This affects derivative coefficients, eigenvalue degree labels and roots-of-unity averages. A monic triangular polynomial basis change can remain invertible even when a factorial-based sampling formula fails. Checking characteristic therefore separates a failure of one formula from a failure of the underlying representation itself.

glossary.definition: The finite product (a)ₙ = a(a+1)⋯(a+n−1), with (a)₀ = 1. This is the Pochhammer convention used in the hypergeometric series entry. The notation must be distinguished from falling factorials and from the step-N factorial lanes.
glossary.quick_example: (2)₃ = 2·3·4 = 24, while the falling factorial 2(2−1)(2−2) is zero.
explanation: The rising factorial advances its factors upward by one, and the zero-length product is one. It provides compact coefficient formulas for hypergeometric series and for rescaled arithmetic-progression products.

Notation is a common source of confusion because some sources use similar parentheses for falling products. Check the displayed factors or the stated Pochhammer convention. Reversing the direction changes roots, signs and recurrence relations, so a familiar-looking symbol alone does not justify importing another source’s formula.

glossary.definition: The coefficient rule for multiplying ordinary formal power series: the coefficient of zⁿ in A(z)B(z) is Σₖ₌₀ⁿ aₖbₙ₋ₖ. Each coefficient uses finitely many terms, so this formal rule needs no analytic convergence assumption.
glossary.quick_example: The coefficient of z² in (1+2z+3z²)(1+4z+5z²) is 5+8+3 = 16.
explanation: The Cauchy product is ordinary series multiplication organized by output degree. Each pair of terms contributes to the degree obtained by adding its two exponents. Collecting those contributions gives the convolution formula for the new coefficient sequence.

This finite-per-coefficient interpretation is automatically meaningful formally. Analytic statements about multiplying convergent numerical sums require their relevant convergence hypotheses. The term also differs from binomial convolution, which appears when the stored coefficients use an exponential rather than ordinary power basis.

glossary.definition: An infinite coefficient list written as Σₙ≥₀ aₙzⁿ and manipulated coefficientwise over a declared ring. Addition and multiplication are algebraic operations on these lists. Evaluating the series at a numerical z is a separate analytic question.
glossary.quick_example: The identity (1−z)(1+z+z²+⋯) = 1 is valid formally even when no numerical value for z is chosen.
explanation: A formal series is treated as its entire coefficient sequence, with equality meaning agreement at every position. The variable is a bookkeeping symbol rather than a numerical input. Infinite notation is harmless for operations whose individual output coefficients have well-defined finite formulas.

This makes formal inversion, residue selection and suitable composition useful independently of analytic convergence. A finite prefix verifies only a finite set of coefficient statements. To evaluate the series or bound a discarded tail at a chosen number, one must supply analytic information beyond the formal algebra.

glossary.definition: For a complex power series centered at zero, the radius R such that the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and diverges for |z| > R. The endpoints R = 0 and R = ∞ are allowed. Boundary convergence must be checked separately.
glossary.quick_example: The geometric series Σₙ≥₀ zⁿ has radius 1. At z = 1 its terms do not tend to zero.
explanation: The radius describes where one complex power series represents a convergent sum around its center. Inside the open disk it converges absolutely; beyond the radius it cannot converge. Boundary points can behave differently from one another and need separate analysis.

The radius does not by itself provide a useful finite-truncation error at every interior point. Evaluation near the boundary may need many terms or stronger coefficient estimates. A formal identity remains valid coefficientwise even when the corresponding numerical substitution lies outside this convergence region.

glossary.definition: For a function analytic near zero, the ordinary coefficient of zⁿ in its Taylor series is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n!. Its exponentially normalized coefficient is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0). The basis convention determines which number is called the stored coefficient.
glossary.quick_example: For exp(z), every derivative at zero is 1, while its ordinary coefficients are 1, 1, 1/2, 1/6, ….
explanation: Taylor coefficients connect local derivative data with a power-series representation. The factorial compensates for differentiating zⁿ exactly n times. Forgetting it confuses an ordinary coefficient list with an exponentially normalized sequence.

Knowing derivatives formally or to finite order does not automatically provide a convergent Taylor representation of a general smooth function. The analytic setting in this definition supplies that interpretation. For a finite approximation, the range of validity and a remainder estimate still need to accompany the retained coefficients.

glossary.definition: The polynomial operator ∇f(x) = f(x)−f(x−1), with unit step. It differs from the forward difference Δf(x) = f(x+1)−f(x). The falling-degree operator is x∇, while the falling-factorial lowering operator is Δ.
glossary.quick_example: For f(x) = x², ∇f = 2x−1 and Δf = 2x+1.
explanation: Backward difference compares the current value with its value one step earlier. It is related to forward difference by translation, but they act differently at the same argument. Their explicit formulas should therefore be preserved when transporting operators or comparing coefficient recurrences.

In the falling-factorial calculus, multiplying the backward difference by x gives the degree operator. The plain backward difference alone is not that degree counter. On finite sampled signals, both directions also require a boundary rule for the sample requested outside the stored range.

glossary.definition: A linear map between algebras that also preserves their specified multiplication; in the unital convention it preserves the identity element. A linear coordinate isomorphism alone need not satisfy the multiplication condition.
glossary.quick_example: The falling-factorial map sends z² to x(x−1), while the square of its value on z is x². It therefore fails to preserve ordinary multiplication.
explanation: Preserving multiplication means that encoding a product agrees with multiplying the encoded factors: Φ(fg)=Φ(f)Φ(g), for the products actually declared. Linearity alone only guarantees compatibility with addition and scalar scaling, so it cannot supply this extra identity.

The falling-factorial coordinate map illustrates the difference: Φ(z²)=x(x−1), while Φ(z)Φ(z)=x² under ordinary multiplication. Defining a transported product on the target restores multiplicative compatibility. This permits the original algebraic laws to travel through the representation without silently changing which product is being used.

glossary.definition: A shift of a finite length-N signal with indices reduced modulo N. Under the convention (Sx)ₙ = xₙ₋₁ mod N, the last sample moves to the first position. This boundary rule differs from zero extension.
glossary.quick_example: The circular delay sends (1,2,3,4) to (4,1,2,3).
explanation: A circular shift treats the finite signal as one period of a repeating sequence. Samples crossing an endpoint reappear at the opposite endpoint, so the operation is a reversible permutation of the stored coordinates and preserves their Euclidean energy.

This boundary behavior distinguishes it from a zero-extended delay, which can discard the final sample and insert zero. Fourier diagonalization and polyphase carry formulas must use the intended convention. Matching the shift’s name or tap pattern is insufficient if the endpoint model changes.

glossary.definition: Retaining samples on a specified residue class: with factor m and phase r, yₖ = xₘₖ₊ᵣ. The phase and boundary convention are part of the operation. Retaining only one phase generally loses information about the others.
glossary.quick_example: Taking the even phase of (1,2,3,4) gives (1,3). Retaining the odd phase (2,4) as well permits interleaving back to the original signal.
explanation: Downsampling keeps one phase of an indexed sequence. It reduces the number of stored samples but generally merges inputs that differ on the discarded phases. The starting residue r matters because changing it selects a different subset.

Keeping all phases as separate streams is instead a reversible polyphase reorganization. Exact recovery from fewer samples can become possible with a restricted signal class or a suitable complete filter bank. Such an input restriction or complementary channel is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of downsampling alone.

glossary.definition: Failure of a sampling operation to distinguish different inputs. In frequency language, distinct oscillations can produce the same retained samples. Additional input restrictions or complementary filter-bank outputs are needed for exact recovery.
glossary.quick_example: On integer indices, the signals 1 and (−1)ⁿ both give the constant sequence 1 after retaining only even-indexed samples.
explanation: Aliasing is a collision in the sampling map. Oscillations that differ before sampling can become indistinguishable afterward, so no algorithm receiving only those samples can recover which unrestricted input was present.

Anti-alias filtering changes the permitted or retained frequency content before downsampling, while multi-channel reconstruction can retain complementary information. These remedies have their own assumptions. Relabeling the sampled frequencies does not restore distinctions that the acquisition process has already removed.

glossary.definition: A collection of filters and sampling maps sending one signal to several component streams. A synthesis bank combines those streams into an output signal. Perfect reconstruction is a property of the combined analysis and synthesis maps with their declared delays and boundary conventions.
glossary.quick_example: For a pair (u,v), the Haar analysis stores average (u+v)/2 and detail (u−v)/2; synthesis returns their sum and difference.
explanation: An analysis bank distributes information across several filtered streams, often followed by phase selection or downsampling. A synthesis bank reconstructs by filtering and combining those streams. Individual streams may be insufficient even when their complete collection retains the original signal.

Perfect reconstruction is an identity of the combined maps, with any allowed delay or scale stated explicitly. It depends on the filters, boundary rules and sampling phases together. Checking each channel separately or retaining only its energy does not establish that joint identity.

glossary.definition: An invertible update of one component using another, such as predicting odd samples from even samples and then updating the even stream with the prediction residual. The inverse undoes the updates in reverse order. This signal-processing meaning of lifting differs from lifting an object through a quotient.
glossary.quick_example: Set d = v−u, then a = u+d/2. Recover u = a−d/2 and v = u+d.
explanation: Lifting builds an invertible transform from simple updates whose inverses are explicit. A predict step stores a discrepancy using another stream; an update step then changes that other stream using the stored discrepancy. Reversing the sequence and subtracting the same updates recovers the inputs.

Normalization can be applied separately from these updates. The prediction residual therefore need not equal the tutorial’s half-difference coefficient without an additional scale and sign conversion. This constructive factorization explains reversibility, but does not by itself imply orthonormality or a particular boundary extension.

glossary.definition: An equality between the squared norm of an object and the correctly weighted squared magnitudes of its complete transform coefficients. Orthonormal coordinates use unit weights. Other normalizations change the weights, so energy formulas must follow the analysis convention.
glossary.quick_example: With a = (u+v)/2 and d = (u−v)/2, u²+v² = 2(a²+d²). The factor 2 belongs to this normalization.
explanation: The identity connects coefficient bookkeeping with the geometry of the original object. For a complete orthonormal transform, every squared coefficient magnitude contributes directly to the total energy. Nonorthonormal but invertible coordinates instead need weights or a metric, potentially including cross terms.

This distinction matters when ranking coefficients for truncation. A large raw coefficient does not necessarily represent a large physical energy contribution under an arbitrary normalization. Exact reconstruction and an additive sum-of-squares identity are separate properties and should each be established for the representation used.

glossary.definition: A rule supplying samples outside the stored finite signal, such as periodic continuation, zero extension or reflection. A filter’s taps do not determine its finite matrix until this rule and the indexing convention have been fixed.
glossary.quick_example: Delaying (1,2,3,4) by one sample gives (0,1,2,3) with zero extension and (4,1,2,3) with circular indexing.
explanation: A boundary convention completes a finite signal into the values needed by a shift or filter near its endpoints. Zero extension inserts zeros, periodic continuation wraps around, and reflection mirrors samples according to its specified endpoint rule.

These choices can agree on interior outputs while disagreeing at the edges. Consequently a test using only interior samples can miss an incorrect finite operator. The convention must travel with any polyphase, wavelet or matrix representation of the filter rather than be supplied silently by an implementation default.

glossary.definition: A quantum system with a two-dimensional complex state space. A pure state has a unit-vector representative α|0⟩+β|1⟩ with |α|²+|β|² = 1; multiplying both amplitudes by one global phase leaves the same density matrix. Mixed states use density matrices.
glossary.quick_example: The vector (3/5,4/5) is normalized because 9/25+16/25 = 1.
explanation: A qubit is a two-dimensional state system, not merely a stored bit with an unknown value. Its pure-state amplitudes can have a relative phase that influences measurements beyond the coordinate basis. Density matrices also allow statistical mixtures of preparations.

The two coordinate probabilities alone do not specify a general qubit state. Measurements in additional settings can detect its off-diagonal entries, which is why tomography uses several settings. A single observed outcome likewise does not reveal the full amplitude or probability list.

glossary.definition: A common unit-modulus factor multiplying every amplitude of a state vector. It cancels in |ψ⟩⟨ψ| and leaves the represented pure-state density matrix unchanged. This statement assumes the factor applies to the whole state being compared.
glossary.quick_example: The vectors (3/5,4/5) and (3i/5,4i/5) give the same density matrix.
explanation: Multiplying a whole state vector by eⁱθ changes its representative but leaves ψψ* unchanged, because the factor and its conjugate cancel. All measurement probabilities derived from that density matrix therefore stay the same.

The word whole is essential. Applying a phase only to one component or one coherent branch changes a relative phase and can alter interference. A factor that is global for an isolated subexpression may become relative when that expression is compared coherently with another branch of a larger state.

glossary.definition: The phase difference between nonzero amplitudes in a chosen basis. It appears in off-diagonal density-matrix entries and can change interference probabilities even when the basis populations stay fixed.
glossary.quick_example: The states (3/5,4/5) and (3/5,−4/5) have the same Z probabilities but X-plus probabilities 49/50 and 1/50.
explanation: Relative phase compares components rather than multiplying the entire state by one common factor. It enters the products of amplitudes appearing off the density matrix’s diagonal. A measurement combining those components can turn that phase information into different outcome probabilities.

The selected basis and nonzero amplitudes matter to the comparison. In the demonstration, changing the phase of the second amplitude leaves Z probabilities fixed but changes X or Y probabilities. Retaining only Z populations therefore cannot recover every phase-sensitive observation.

glossary.definition: A density matrix of the form ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| for a unit vector ψ. In finite dimensions it has rank one, satisfies ρ² = ρ and has purity tr(ρ²) = 1. The vector representative is determined only up to global phase.
explanation: A pure-state density matrix is the orthogonal projector onto one normalized state direction. The unit-vector representative carries no additional information through its overall phase, which is why different phase representatives give the same projector.

Purity can be recognized from ρ²=ρ or tr(ρ²)=1 in the finite trace-one positive setting. A deterministic unitary evolution preserves this property. A channel that discards information about branches can instead produce a mixed output, even when its input was pure.

glossary.definition: A density matrix that is not pure. In finite dimensions its purity is less than one, and it can be written as a convex mixture of pure-state density matrices. Such a decomposition is generally not unique.
glossary.quick_example: The dephased state diag(9/25,16/25) has purity 337/625, so it is mixed.
explanation: A mixed state is represented by a convex combination of pure-state density matrices, with nonnegative weights summing to one. It can arise from uncertain preparation or from forgetting part of a larger system or measurement record.

Different preparation ensembles can yield the same density matrix and therefore the same state-level measurement probabilities. The mixture should not be confused with adding state amplitudes coherently: probabilities average across an ensemble, whereas amplitude addition can introduce interference cross terms.

glossary.definition: A Hermitian operator E satisfying 0 ≤ E ≤ I. For density matrix ρ, tr(Eρ) is the probability of its associated outcome. Effects in a complete measurement sum to I. They need not individually be projectors.
glossary.quick_example: E = I/2 gives probability 1/2 for every state, although E² = I/4 differs from E.
explanation: An effect describes the probability question associated with one outcome. The inequalities 0≤E≤I ensure that its probability lies between zero and one for every state. A complete measurement consists of effects whose sum is I.

A projector is a special effect with the additional idempotence property. General effects can describe less sharp measurements and need not identify a post-measurement state by themselves. The probability rule and the state-update rule are separate pieces of a measurement model.

glossary.definition: In the finite setting, a Hermitian operator whose real eigenvalues label possible outcomes of its projective measurement. Its expectation in state ρ is tr(Aρ). The operator and its measurement effects have related but different roles.
glossary.quick_example: The Pauli matrix Z = diag(1,−1) has mean 9/25−16/25 = −7/25 in the demonstration state.
explanation: An observable packages numerical outcome labels together with their spectral projectors. The Born probabilities determine how likely those outcomes are, and their weighted average equals tr(Aρ). Its expectation is therefore a summary of a measurement distribution, not necessarily an individual outcome.

Different observables ask different questions about the same state. The Pauli X, Y and Z settings in the example reveal different combinations of its entries. Noncommuting observables need not share a measurement basis, so their probability descriptions cannot be identified simply by reusing coordinate populations.

glossary.definition: A linear completely positive, trace-preserving map on density matrices. A finite Kraus representation is Φ(ρ) = ΣⱼKⱼρKⱼ* with ΣⱼKⱼ*Kⱼ = I. Complete positivity requires positivity to survive extension by an arbitrary auxiliary quantum system.
glossary.quick_example: Coordinate dephasing uses K₀ = diag(1,0) and K₁ = diag(0,1), keeping the diagonal entries and deleting the off-diagonal entries.
explanation: A channel describes an unconditioned physical state transformation in the finite model. Complete positivity ensures that the operation remains valid when applied to one part of a larger quantum system, while trace preservation retains total probability.

Unitary evolution is one channel, but dephasing and damping can lose information. A channel need not have a physically valid inverse even when one can write a formal linear inverse on some subset of matrices. Selected measurement branches also require conditioning and are not individually trace-preserving channels in general.

glossary.definition: Reconstructing a state from probabilities for a sufficiently informative collection of measurement settings. For a qubit, exact X, Y and Z outcome probabilities determine its density matrix. Experimental estimates introduce sampling error and must still describe a positive state.
glossary.quick_example: For the phase-one demonstration state, X-plus = 49/50, Y-plus = 1/2 and Z-plus = 9/25 recover the upper-right entry 12/25.
glossary.note: One outcome from a single copy does not supply the three ensemble probabilities.
explanation: Tomography treats measurement probabilities as a representation of the unknown state. Informationally sufficient settings permit reconstruction of all its independent matrix parameters. For a qubit, X, Y and Z settings provide the three real parameters left after Hermitian symmetry and trace normalization.

The demonstration uses exact ensemble probabilities, so inversion is an exact algebraic calculation. Experimental frequencies are estimates and can yield an unconstrained reconstructed matrix that is not positive. Statistical uncertainty and state-validity constraints must therefore be handled in an actual estimation procedure.

glossary.definition: A projective measurement with its outcome retained. Outcome j has probability pⱼ = tr(Pⱼρ); if pⱼ > 0, the conditional output state is PⱼρPⱼ/pⱼ. Discarding the outcome instead gives the sum ΣⱼPⱼρPⱼ.
glossary.quick_example: In the demonstration, retaining coordinate outcome zero gives the state |0⟩⟨0| with probability 9/25.
glossary.note: The conditional state formula is undefined for a zero-probability outcome.
explanation: Retaining an outcome tells us which branch occurred. Dividing PⱼρPⱼ by its nonzero probability renormalizes that branch into a trace-one conditional state. This conditional state can differ from the unconditioned state obtained by averaging over all outcomes.

If the outcome is discarded, the branch probabilities are already included in the unnormalized terms, so those terms are summed directly. Confusing the normalized selected branches with their weighted unconditioned sum gives an incorrect channel or incorrect probabilities. Zero-probability branches cannot be normalized by this formula.

glossary.definition: The complex voltage-to-current ratio of a linear one-port at a stated frequency, written Z = R+iX. Its real part is resistance and its imaginary part is reactance. The Smith-chart guide uses a positive real reference resistance Z₀ and normalized impedance z = Z/Z₀.
glossary.quick_example: The load Z = 25+i25 ohms with Z₀ = 50 ohms has normalized impedance z = (1+i)/2.
explanation: Impedance describes the joint magnitude and phase relation between voltage and current in the stated linear frequency-domain model. Resistance contributes its real part, while reactance contributes its imaginary part. Both generally depend on the frequency at which the load is examined.

The Smith chart changes coordinates from impedance to reflection; it does not change the physical load. A single-frequency impedance value also differs from an entire rational impedance function Z(s). Matching a value at one frequency is therefore a weaker request than realizing a prescribed function across its domain.

glossary.definition: The dimensionless ratio z = Z/Z₀ relative to a declared reference impedance. In the Smith-chart guide Z₀ is positive and real, so the real and imaginary parts are normalized resistance and reactance.
glossary.quick_example: Changing Z₀ from 50 to 25 ohms changes the coordinates of a 50-ohm resistor from z = 1 to z = 2, while the physical resistor stays the same.
explanation: Normalization measures the load relative to the chosen reference, removing its physical units from the chart coordinates. The same physical impedance can occupy different normalized positions when Z₀ changes. A normalized value of one means equality with that reference.

The guide assumes a positive real reference resistance, which supports its familiar passive-disk and return-loss formulas. More general complex-reference conventions require their own definitions. Physical component values must also be converted consistently when moving between normalized circuit formulas and a dimensional implementation.

glossary.definition: The reciprocal Y = 1/Z where Z is nonzero, measured in siemens. With normalized impedance z, normalized admittance is y = 1/z. Switching to the admittance grid changes the description of the same load.
glossary.quick_example: If z = (1+i)/2, then y = 1−i.
glossary.note: A short has zero impedance and no finite reciprocal admittance.
explanation: Admittance describes the same one-port using current per voltage instead of voltage per current. Parallel combinations are often simpler in this description, just as series combinations are simpler in impedance coordinates. The reciprocal relation must still respect zeros and poles.

On the normalized chart, the admittance reflection coordinate is the negative of the impedance reflection coordinate under the stated convention. Switching grids therefore changes the coordinate description, not the load. An ideal short or open needs limiting treatment rather than a finite reciprocal value in both descriptions.

glossary.definition: For normalized impedance z with z ≠ −1, the Smith coordinate Γ = (z−1)/(z+1). For finite passive loads with nonnegative resistance, |Γ| ≤ 1. Its magnitude measures mismatch relative to the declared positive real reference resistance.
explanation: The reflection coordinate converts the positive-real load half-plane into a disk. Its center represents a match, and its boundary represents the ideal passive zero-resistance limit together with the open-load limiting point. Both magnitude and phase are needed to specify a general chart position.

The magnitude is especially useful because a lossless line preserves it. Equal magnitudes therefore place loads on the same continuous line-rotation circle, but a prescribed finite cyclic action can impose further phase restrictions. Reflection data at one frequency do not alone identify a unique broadband circuit.

glossary.definition: The fractional-linear coordinate map Γ = (z−1)/(z+1) and its inverse z = (1+Γ)/(1−Γ), on their stated domains. It takes the open positive-real half-plane to the open unit disk and finite purely reactive impedances to its boundary.
glossary.quick_example: The matched point z = 1 maps to Γ = 0. The point Γ = 1 has no finite impedance under the inverse formula.
glossary.note: Other literature uses different Cayley-transform conventions. Keep this direction and reference normalization explicit.
explanation: The Cayley map is reversible away from its excluded denominator zeros. It allows a geometric statement in the reflection disk to be translated into an impedance-coordinate statement in a half-plane. For example, rotating Γ becomes a fractional-linear action on z after conjugating by the coordinate map.

Boundary behavior requires care because finite disk coordinates can correspond to an infinite impedance limit. The point Γ=1 is a pole of the inverse formula. Treating it as an ordinary finite load can invalidate arithmetic or a claimed packet decomposition at that point.

glossary.definition: A load with impedance equal to the chosen reference resistance in this real-reference model. Its normalized impedance is z = 1 and its reflection coefficient is zero. Matching is relative to the reference and frequency being used.
glossary.quick_example: A 50-ohm resistor is matched to a 50-ohm real reference and gives VSWR 1.
explanation: A match eliminates reflection at the chosen reference plane in this model. It fixes both the resistance and reactance requirements: the load equals the positive real Z₀, rather than merely having a convenient resistance magnitude.

Matching depends on frequency and reference conventions. A lossless line can rotate a nonzero reflection coefficient but cannot change its magnitude to zero, so line rotation alone cannot match an arbitrary mismatched load. Adding a matching network poses a different realization problem with additional permitted operations and components.

glossary.definition: For reflection magnitude r with 0 ≤ r < 1, VSWR = (1+r)/(1−r). The matched case gives one; as r approaches one the ratio diverges. The ideal passive boundary is assigned infinite VSWR.
glossary.quick_example: Reflection magnitude 1/3 gives VSWR 2.
explanation: VSWR converts reflection magnitude into the ratio between standing-wave voltage maxima and minima in the ideal line model. Its value loses the reflection phase, so many different loads have the same VSWR. The ratio grows sharply as the reflection magnitude approaches the passive boundary.

A finite VSWR greater than one signals mismatch relative to the reference, but does not identify which impedance or matching operation is needed. The matched value one and the infinite boundary limit should be handled separately rather than substituted blindly into formulas involving division by 1−r.

glossary.definition: For 0 < |Γ| ≤ 1, the quantity −20 log₁₀|Γ| in decibels. Smaller reflected magnitude gives larger return loss. The matched limit |Γ| = 0 has ideal infinite return loss; the passive boundary |Γ| = 1 gives zero decibels.
glossary.quick_example: For |Γ| = 1/√5, return loss is 10 log₁₀5, approximately 6.99 decibels.
explanation: Return loss expresses reflected amplitude on a logarithmic decibel scale under the stated convention. The minus sign makes a smaller reflection magnitude correspond to a larger positive return-loss value. It therefore moves in the opposite numerical direction from mismatch measures that increase with reflection.

Like VSWR, it omits reflection phase and does not identify the load uniquely. The infinite matched limit is an ideal mathematical value, not a finite measured number. Comparing return-loss values requires the same reference and a compatible measurement or model convention.

glossary.definition: In the guide’s propagation convention, a line of length ℓ gives Γin = ΓL exp(−4πiℓ/λ) at wavelength λ. It rotates the reflection point while preserving its magnitude. This is a physical line model with its own length and reference assumptions.
glossary.quick_example: A quarter wavelength multiplies Γ by −1 and sends a finite nonzero normalized load z to 1/z.
glossary.note: Line rotation alone cannot turn a nonzero reflection magnitude into a matched load.
explanation: Propagation changes the phase accumulated by the reflected wave on a round trip. This explains the factor 4πℓ/λ in the guide’s reflection formula. A quarter-wavelength changes the reflection sign and, where finite, reciprocates normalized impedance.

Because the magnitude is unchanged, line propagation has an exact reachability limitation: it moves along a reflection circle rather than throughout the disk. This physical model is also distinct from choosing one of N algebraic cyclic rotations. Their phases can coincide at selected lengths without making their allowed action sets identical.

glossary.definition: Reachability by a fixed finite set of phase rotations Γ ↦ ωᴷΓ, where ω = exp(2πi/N), N > 0 and K is an integer. For Γ₀ ≠ 0, a target Γ* is reachable exactly when (Γ*/Γ₀)ᴺ = 1. The zero start reaches only zero.
glossary.quick_example: For N = 4, the orbit of Γ₀ = 1/2 is {1/2,i/2,−1/2,−i/2}. A point at angle π/4 with radius 1/2 is outside this orbit.
explanation: The allowed orbit contains only the N equally spaced phase multiples of the starting point, with repetitions removed in degenerate cases. For a nonzero start, dividing by Γ₀ isolates the required phase factor. Raising it to N tests whether that factor is one of the allowed roots of unity.

Matching radius is therefore necessary but generally insufficient for fixed finite N. The zero start is a separate case because division by Γ₀ is unavailable and every rotation fixes zero. Increasing the allowed order changes the reachability problem rather than proving reachability under the original order.

glossary.definition: A point where a rational function has a nonremovable singularity after common factors are cancelled. A zero in a displayed denominator is only a candidate until cancellation is considered. Individual terms in a decomposition can have poles that cancel in their sum.
glossary.quick_example: The function 1/(1−t) has a pole at t = 1. By contrast, (1−t)/(1−t) extends to the constant 1 after cancellation.
explanation: A pole is a genuine blow-up of the reduced rational function near a point, not merely a denominator zero in one unreduced formula. Cancelling common factors can reveal that an apparent singularity was removable.

Decomposed expressions need additional care: individual packet terms can have poles whose singular parts cancel when summed. Evaluating those terms separately at the singular point can therefore fail even when the total extends regularly. State whether a formula concerns each component, their sum or a limiting continuation.

glossary.definition: A quotient of polynomials over a declared field, understood with common factors cancelled when studying its poles or degree. In circuit work the variable is often complex frequency s. Frequency samples alone do not determine an arbitrary rational function without further constraints.
glossary.quick_example: The one-inductor example has normalized impedance z(s) = (7s+5)/(2s+4).
explanation: A rational function is an exact global algebraic description, subject to its domain exclusions. Its values are determined by numerator and denominator polynomials up to common rescaling and cancellation. Degree and pole questions should use a reduced representation.

Finitely many samples generally permit many rational interpolants when degree and other restrictions are unspecified. Additional conditions such as passivity, analyticity, properness or bounded degree change the admissible class. Finding one fitting formula does not establish uniqueness or a realization within every circuit topology.

glossary.definition: In the real-rational scalar circuit setting, a rational function Z(s) analytic for Re s > 0 and satisfying Re Z(s) ≥ 0 there. Real coefficients give the usual conjugation symmetry. Boundary poles and realization restrictions require their stated additional conditions.
glossary.quick_example: For positive R and L, the series RL function Z(s) = R+sL has positive real part throughout Re s > 0.
glossary.note: Checking finitely many frequency samples is insufficient to establish positivity on the whole half-plane.
explanation: Positive-realness encodes a half-plane positivity condition on an entire function, not only on selected boundary samples. In passive network theory it connects analytic impedance behavior with realizability under appropriate classical assumptions.

A restricted synthesis question can impose more requirements, such as positive element values, a particular topology or no transformers. Those restrictions should remain separate from the analytic positive-real test. A finite sample check can detect a violation at a sampled point but cannot generally certify the whole half-plane condition.

glossary.definition: A complex analytic function F on the open unit disk satisfying |F(t)| ≤ 1 throughout that disk. The Smith-chart research uses such reflection functions for interpolation. A rational Schur function has a finite rational description, with its degree and boundary behavior still to be specified.
glossary.quick_example: F(t) = t is a Schur function. It realizes the sample values 1/2 at t = 1/2 and −1/2 at t = −1/2.
explanation: A Schur function remains inside the closed unit disk in value while its argument ranges over the open disk. This global analytic constraint makes interpolation much more restrictive than passing a polynomial through finitely many prescribed points.

The Cayley-coordinate viewpoint relates such bounded reflection functions to half-plane positivity under the relevant transformations. Rationality and degree are extra properties. A Schur interpolation witness therefore need not supply a circuit with a requested component count or a specific transformer-free realization.

glossary.definition: Finding a function in a declared class that takes prescribed values at prescribed nodes. Feasibility, uniqueness and the range of possible unmeasured values are separate questions. A fit in an unrestricted polynomial class need not satisfy the analytic or passive constraints of a circuit model.
glossary.quick_example: The data F(1/2) = 1/2 and F(−1/2) = −1/2 admit F(t) = t in the Schur class.
explanation: Interpolation first asks whether the requested values can be attained within a specified function class. Once feasible, one can ask whether the interpolant is unique, what other values it can take or how small its degree can be.

These are separate questions because finite data may leave substantial freedom. The Schur class adds a global analytic bound, and a restricted circuit class adds still further structure. A fit in a larger class cannot automatically answer feasibility or uniqueness in the smaller one.

glossary.definition: For distinct disk nodes tₖ and proposed scalar values vₖ, the Hermitian matrix Pₖₗ = (1−vₖ conjugate(vₗ))/(1−tₖ conjugate(tₗ)). Its positive semidefiniteness is the classical scalar Schur interpolation criterion used in the linked reading.
glossary.quick_example: The nodes 1/2 and −1/2 with equal respective values give P = [[1,1],[1,1]], a rank-one singular matrix.
glossary.note: The nodes are distinct and strictly inside the disk. This criterion is not a component-count theorem for a restricted circuit topology.
explanation: The matrix combines the proposed values with the geometry of their disk nodes. Its positive-semidefinite condition tests whether those finite observations can come from a scalar Schur function under the theorem’s hypotheses. It is more informative than checking only that each individual value lies in the disk.

Singularity is a meaningful boundary case, not merely a numerical inconvenience. Null vectors can force additional constraints on an unmeasured value. A tolerance-based eigenvalue decision needs care near that boundary, and the interpolation criterion still does not settle restricted physical component-count questions.

glossary.definition: For Hermitian P ≥ 0, the block matrix [[P,b],[b*,d]] is positive semidefinite exactly when b is perpendicular to ker P and d ≥ b*P†b. Here P† is the Moore–Penrose inverse. The range condition remains essential when P is singular.
glossary.quick_example: If P = 0, its range is {0}. Positivity of the augmented block forces b = 0 as well as d ≥ 0.
glossary.note: Substituting a pseudoinverse into the scalar inequality while omitting the range condition is insufficient.
explanation: At a singular positive-semidefinite block, the new column must avoid directions in the old kernel. Otherwise the augmented quadratic form can become negative regardless of the lower-right scalar. This explains why the range condition is logically independent of the remaining pseudoinverse inequality.

After the range condition holds, completing the square reduces positivity to d−b*P†b≥0. If P=0, the condition forces b=0 outright. When P itself depends on unknown data, its pseudoinverse cannot be treated as a fixed known matrix while varying those data.

glossary.definition: For a proper scalar rational transfer function p(s)/q(s) in lowest terms, the degree of q. It counts the minimal state dimension of an unrestricted finite linear realization. Improper functions and restricted passive circuit component counts need their own conventions.
glossary.quick_example: The proper function (7s+5)/(2s+4) has no common numerator-denominator factor and has McMillan degree one.
glossary.note: A minimal state dimension does not alone give the minimum number of reactive elements in a transformer-free network.
explanation: In the stated proper scalar setting, cancelling common factors identifies the genuinely retained denominator dynamics. Its degree corresponds to the smallest state dimension among unrestricted finite linear realizations of that transfer function.

This is an input-output complexity measure, not a universal count of circuit elements. A passive network with restricted components or forbidden transformers can need a different analysis. An approximation with smaller McMillan degree also realizes a different function unless an exact equality with the target is established.

glossary.definition: A network built from the allowed components whose driving-point impedance or transfer function equals the specified function on its stated domain. The component alphabet, positivity rules and permitted transformers determine the realization problem.
glossary.quick_example: The linked one-inductor example uses a series resistor 5/4 followed by a parallel resistor 9/4 and inductor 9/8 in normalized units.
glossary.note: An approximation by a lower-degree function is a realization of the approximating function. It does not establish an exact lower-component realization of the target.
explanation: A circuit realization must reproduce the specified impedance or transfer behavior using the permitted component laws. Topology, element values and admissibility restrictions all belong to the construction. Two algebraically equivalent rational expressions need not display the same circuit directly.

Existence of an unrestricted state-space model or a Schur interpolant is therefore only part of a restricted synthesis argument. Exact realization, approximation quality and minimum component count are distinct claims. The one-inductor supplement explicitly realizes its degree-one approximation without settling the harder exact higher-degree target question.

glossary.definition: A description of a discrete linear system by xₙ₊₁ = Axₙ+Buₙ and yₙ = Cxₙ+Duₙ. It declares the retained state x, input u and observation y. Different coordinate systems can describe the same input-output behavior.
glossary.quick_example: The hidden-memory example has full state (y,z) and autonomous update matrix [[1,1],[1,0]]. Its visible observation selects y.
explanation: The state stores the information used to continue the system, while the observation extracts the quantity reported externally. Inputs affect the next state through B and can contribute immediately to the output through D. The matrices therefore have different typed roles despite appearing in one model.

An invertible state-coordinate change can preserve input-output behavior while changing these stored matrices. Minimal state dimension and restricted physical realization are additional questions. Observing y alone also need not provide a sufficient state, because distinct hidden states can share the same current output.

glossary.term: State sufficient for a deterministic update
glossary.definition: A retained value that determines its own next value for every admissible full state, under a specified deterministic evolution. If R is the summary and T the full update, this requires a map T̄ with T̄R = RT on the admissible states.
glossary.quick_example: In the Fibonacci update, y alone is insufficient, while (yₙ,yₙ₋₁) has the autonomous rule (u,v) ↦ (u+v,u).
glossary.note: Stochastic Markov properties concern conditional distributions and require their own probability model.
explanation: In this deterministic use, the retained value contains everything needed for the next update. The factorization T̄R=RT says that updating the full state and then summarizing agrees with updating the summary directly.

The condition must hold for every admissible state, not merely one observed trajectory. Adding an appropriate delayed value can make an insufficient summary sufficient, as in the hidden-memory example. Stochastic Markov properties instead concern conditional probability laws and require a probability model beyond this deterministic criterion.

glossary.definition: An input x satisfying T(x) = x for a declared map T. For a linear projector P, the fixed points are precisely its image. Being fixed is an algebraic property; stability under nearby perturbations is a further question.
glossary.quick_example: The projector P(x,y) = (x,0) fixes every point on the horizontal axis.
explanation: A fixed point is unchanged by one application, so it remains unchanged under every repeated application of the same map. For a projector, every output is fixed, which is why its fixed-point set equals its image.

Existence of a fixed point does not establish uniqueness or attraction. Nearby states can move away even when the fixed state itself stays put. Stability and convergence toward a fixed point depend on additional properties of the dynamics and on the neighborhood and metric being considered.

glossary_start.description: Identify the system, the allowed action and the data that generate it.
See how an object splits into selected components.
